Is the government considering implementation of the recommendation made in the report of the restrictive trade practices commission on the manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs as to "the advisability of bringing under the supervision of the food and drug directorate all advertising and promotion activities related to drugs, including the distribution of samples and the content of advertising literature", and the establishment "under the auspices of the federal government, of an authoritative publication giving all necessary particulars concerning new drugs"?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The Food and Drugs Act, which is administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare, has provided considerable authority for a number of years to regulate the labelling and advertising of drugs. This authority is designed to prevent the false or misleading advertising of drugs, and the existing authority is quite broad and comprehensive in this field.
The 1962 amendment of the Food and Drugs Act clearly prohibits the distribution of drug samples to the public and also provides for a regulated distribution of drug samples to physicians, veterinarians, dentists and pharmacists. Regulations have been promulgated that set forth the conditions under which samples may be distributed to members of these professions.
The recommendation of the restrictive trade practices commission that an authoritative publication of new drugs be produced under the auspices of the federal government is still under consideration by the Department of National Health and Welfare.

subtopic: STAFF OF FOOD AND DRUG DIRECTORATE
STAFF OF FOOD AND DRUG DIRECTORATE
speechtext: Is the government considering implementation of the recommendation made in report of the restrictive trade practices commission on the manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs that "the staff of the food and drug directorate should be enlarged considerably to ensure thorough enforcement of the regulations"?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STAFF OF FOOD AND DRUG DIRECTORATE
speechtext: The establishment of the food and drug directorate has been increased to over 500 in the current fiscal year through the addition of 102 new positions. Further staff increases in future years are now being considered by the Department of National Health and Welfare and the treasury board.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The amendments during the past year to the food and drug regulations will be effective in achieving most of the objectives of the recommendations that were cited in the inquiry. More specifically, all premises producing drugs for sale in Canada are subject to inspection by the food and drug directorate. Regulations have been passed during the past year governing the manufacturing processes and quality control procedures in these drug manufacturing plants. Regulations concerning new drugs have been extensively revised, and substantial evidence of effectiveness is now specifically required to be included in the new drug submission. Samples of imported and domestically produced drugs are analysed and examined by the food and drug directorate. Without a tremendous increase in the staff and facilities of the food and drug directorate, however, its analyses cannot establish with certainty that every batch of prescription drugs sold in Canada meet minimum standards of purity and therapeutic efficacy. Also, as a matter of principle, the directorate should not assume the role of production control laboratory for drug manufacturers. The work of the food and drug directorate does encourage the manufacturers, however, to conscientiously fulfil their responsibility for the purity and efficacy of their drug products.
The regulations under the Food and Drugs Act have required for many years that the

Questions
proper name of single drugs and officially designated compound drugs be clearly and prominently displayed on the label in type not less that one half the size of the brand name. In addition, the regulations require a readily discernible quantitative statement of the medicinal ingredients to be included on the labels of compound ethical drugs.
The possibility of identifying all compound drugs with officially designated proper names has been considered several times. It is believed that such an approach would only create more confusion, however, because of the infinite variety of compound drugs that differ both in constituents and in their proportions.
This and other aspects of drug labelling and advertising are being frequently reviewed in the light of the experience gained in administering the Food and Drugs Act and of the views of other interested parties.

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STEPS TO MEET REPORTED INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition has raised a serious question and I would like to be allowed to give a full reply because of the implications that it has.
First of all I will deal with the point about monetary policy. As I have already informed the house, the monetary policy followed in Canada is that which the government and the Bank of Canada consider to be in the best interests of the Canadian economy. This policy is directed and has, I think, been successfully directed to encouraging domestic economic expansion and achieving balance in our international transactions.
Under the policy which has been followed, the money supply in Canada has increased to meet the growing needs of an expanding economy. During the 12 month period ending in November the total currency and bank deposits in Canada, that is the total money supply, has increased by 8.6 per cent, while the privately held money supply has increased by 6.9 per cent. It may be of interest to hon. members to point out that the corresponding increases for the United States over the same period were 7.3 per cent for the total of currency and bank deposits and 8.4 per cent for the privately held money supply, so defined.
The increase in the total currency and bank deposits in Canada over the past two years has amounted to an aggregate figure of 12.9 per cent, which compares with a 15.0 per cent increase in the United States.
In judging the appropriateness of developments in the money supply one must of course take into account a wide variety of factors, including the movement of employment and production, the amount of unused capacity, the state of the balance of payments and so on. The movement of prices is clearly an object of continuous concern, and the monetary authorities must always be alert to upward pressures on the cost of living.
In this respect the recent Canadian experience has compared favourably with most other countries, particularly when account is taken of the devaluation of the Canadian dollar which, though it was helpful in restoring our international competitive position, inevitably had the effect of raising some import prices. Over the recent 12 month period for which information is available the consumer price index rose by 1.6 per cent in Canada, which compares with 1.1 per cent in the United States, 1.3 per cent in the United Kingdom, 6.4 per cent in France and 2.0 per cent in Germany.

speechtext: Order. House again in committee of supply, Department of Post Office, vote No. 1. Shall the item carry?
Are we going to have a statement from the minister?

In presenting the estimates for the department for this year, I can surely not be accused of patronage since these estimates have been initiated and prepared by our honourable friends opposite.
Under these circumstances, naturally, you will permit me to be somewhat restricted in my praise, while being fair towards my coworkers by chance.
Since the annual report of the department for the year 1962-63 has not yet been tabled- it is at the printers-I will allow myself to outline the most important points, then to comment on our 1963-64 estimates, and finally, to inform the house of the initiation of reforms and decisions undertaken by the department since the coming into power of the present

government, and in doing this, I will necessarily limit the number outlined in order not to prolong the debate.
The year 1962-63 was to the Post Office Department, a most significant year of re-organization. Following the report of the royal commission on government organization, every effort was made to incorporate those recommendations of the commission which pertained to the department and which were under the department's jurisdiction.
The changes made emphasized, to a great extent, the decentralization of authority and responsibility to the benefit of officers in the field. As a result, many decisions will be made in the field, providing better service to the public, as field officers will be empowered to make many decisions on the spot rather than wait for approval from headquarters. The changeover is also expected to eliminate much correspondence between headquarters and the field. Headquarters, of course, still remain responsible for formulation of policy and headquarters officers will be in a better position to spend more time on this aspect of the work.
The 1962-63 fiscal year shows total receipts amounting to $222,358,848 while our disbursements totalled $218,872,399 leaving a surplus of $3,486,449.
This compares quite favourably with the figures recorded in 1960-61 and 1961-62, which showed deficits in round figures of $4.7 million and $1.2 million respectively. We must, however, take into account salary increases to post office personnel, which amount to $230,000 and which must be charged to the year 1961-62 and credited to the year 1962-63. On the other hand, we must also debit the retroactive part, amounting to $4,887,076, of the recent salary increases paid during the current year, which should be charged to the fiscal year 1962-63. These retroactive increases produce a real deficit of about $1 million for that year, rather than the surplus of about $3.5 million.

Letter carrier service was inaugurated at Summerside, P.E.I., Oromocto, N.B., Thornhill, Ontario, Ste. Rose, Quebec and Hawkes-bury, Ontario. In addition, 207 additional letter carrier walks were placed in operation, bringing to 3,113,765 the number of calls where letter carriers provide door to door mail delivery. The increase in the number of calls is less than in previous years. This is a result of the reduced expenditure program undertaken by the government during the year under review. The 5,640 rural routes now in operation across Canada have brought this service to an all-time high, serving 645,115 householders.

Post office activities in the field of labour relations saw improved procedures in regard to truck drivers who are employed by contractors for major mail transportation services. Clauses have been inserted in the post office contracts with carriers establishing a minimum hourly wage determined by the Department of Labour. Other clauses incorporated in the contracts deal with annual holidays with pay.
During the year the volume of mail handled showed an increase of 3.94 per cent over the figures for 1961-62. It should be noted that, due to increased efficiency and more effective planning, this increased volume of mail was handled by a staff increase of only one half of one per cent.
The increases and improvements in service that I have described-in letter carrier service, in rural route service, in mail volume and in revenue figures-are the result of the normal growth of the postal service in an expanding economy and a growing population. These increases have been accompanied by an increase in the costs of salaries, transportation and equipment, which are also a normal product of an expanding service.
This pattern of normal growth is reflected in the statistical review of the year 1962-63. While these statistics will be presented in detail on the tabling of the Postmaster General's report, I should like to mention just a few of them here. For instance, departmental revenues increased by almost $9 million in 1962-63 over the previous year. Similarly, departmental expenditures increased by about $4 million during the same period. These figures do not, as I mentioned earlier, include back-dated salary increases which result in a net deficit for the year.

So much for the past. The total departmental estimates for 1963-64 are $191,704,000, which represent an increase of $1,113,500 over last year, taking into consideration supple-mentaries for both years. It should be noted that salary and transportation increases, factors over which the department has little control, account for the bulk of this figure, which has only been kept down to this level by savings made in these and other areas of expenditures.
Our increased expenditures will be met to a large extent by increased postal rates and fees which I announced some months ago. With the new rates, we have calculated that the department will about break even over the next three-year period. It should be noted that without the recent increases, the department's anticipated deficit over the next three years would have been nearly $15 million.

I should like to point out that the five separate rate increases recently announced were all for services which were not paying their way. Under the new rates, there will still be a net loss, but it will be much less.
I have indicated that normal additional services, particularly in regard to letter carrier service, had been slowed down by the government's reduced expenditure program.
I am pleased to tell you that part of the additional revenue from the recent rate increase is being used to provide door-to-door mail delivery on a normal basis which will give this type of service to some 20,000 new homes in the immediate future. Already, since the beginning of October more than
10.000	householders have been granted door-to-door letter carrier delivery service and the others will follow as quickly as arrangements can be completed.
I also intend to give a brand new look to Canadian postage stamps and, in the future, Canadians can look for brighter and more interesting stamps as the department produces three and perhaps four colour stamps by a combination of steel engraving and offset lithography as compared to the customary one or two colour designs. Red will be mostly used to make them more attractive.
We plan to begin a series of coloured stamps showing the various provincial floral emblems. We have under way what I think are attractive stamps on the themes of world peace and Canadian unity, and also stamps to commemorate the Charlottetown and Quebec conferences of 1864 which led to confederation. We have decided, for next year, to issue a special Christmas stamp that should be most appropriate.
The department has in its vaults some
58.000	foreign stamps. We wish to display this magnificent collection for the public. This vast collection is now being catalogued and organized and, we hope, will soon be made available for public inspection both at Ottawa and at other points across the country.
Since becoming Postmaster General I have met with great pleasure every group of postal employees who wanted to meet me. In addition, I have met with the executive officers of all the postal associations. I have also done everything I could to back up the work of the department's standing committee on employee relations. As a proof of my interest in the welfare of the employees, I have succeeded in increasing the percentage of the salary increases granted to postmasters of smaller offices during the recent pay revisions.
Another example of my interest in the welfare of the employees was my decision to give the postmasters of smaller offices an

Supply-Post Office
opportunity to compete for promotion in a wider field, and that, at the request of their association.

Mr. Chairman, would the
minister allow me to ask him a question?
Certainly.
The minister referred to the fact that he had obtained salary increases for the postmasters. Can he tell us the amounts of those raises?

Mr. Chairman, I said that I had succeeded in increasing the percentage of salary increases granted to postmasters of smaller offices. As a rule, the increase is based on a percentage and as these were smaller offices, the increase would have been between $25 or $30, for instance. That is why they were granted, through my intervention, a minimum raise of $60.
That is very good.

Mr. Chairman, at this point in my remarks, I wish to state that, in spite of everything that was said here and elsewhere, the appointment of postmasters and the granting of contracts for supplies and services were made, and still are, under the provisions of the Post Office Act. In all cases, the act was followed faithfully.
Mr. Chairman, I cannot close my remarks without paying a special tribute to all the postal employees who, day in day out, through unselfish devotion to their work, have given the Canada post office a reputation of being second to none. This includes not only the regular employees of the department, but also, the rural mail carriers, the contractors and their employees, whose contribution to the postal service is great indeed.
In short, the Post Office Department has given and continues to give to the Canadian people a service of which they can be proud, and it is for this reason that I humbly ask this house to approve the estimates, as now submitted.

Mr. Chairman, my first words will be to congratulate the minister for having been as brief in his remarks as his administration will be.
We noted that the Postmaster General (Mr. Denis) came into the house under a certain nervous stress, probably dreading the moment where we could at last criticize his department.
The minister has colour and all hon. members know him, but what we would like to know is the political colour of those he seems to favour in certain very special circumstances.
[Mr. Denis.1
Mr. Chairman, the attendance of the Postmaster General in the house this afternoon was prepared by the Secretary of State and leader of the house (Mr. Pickersgill), who is known for his wit during our discussions. Indeed, as found on page 5733 of Hansard of December 11, 1963, the leader of the house announced that we would benefit from the lights of the Postmaster General. Here is what he said:
When they have concluded-
And the leader of the house had just been speaking about the Department of Agriculture.
-and the carnage is over, the Postmaster General is only too ready to enter the slaughter house.
Those are the words used by the leader of the house and I think he was right. I do not think the Postmaster General will enter the slaughter house, but I think that he is ready to commit suicide to try and save the reputation of the Liberal party.
At this stage of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I avail myself of the opportunity to tell the minister I understand his great selfdenial in face of the patronage situation experienced in his department, in so few weeks of administration. The minister will not mind, I hope, if I tell him I understand he has already made his sublime sacrifice on the altar of Liberal patronage and that he is ready to tell his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), like St. Theresa of Lisieux: It does not matter, my God, if I burn in hell for eternity, if such is the will of the dear leader of the Liberal party.
Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister is ready for holocaust, so much so that he omitted, in his introduction, to speak about the most important problems-
One sees the mote in other people's eyes, but does not see the beam in his own.

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) would abide by standing orders, I would be grateful to him. No doubt, he has interesting things to tell us, and if they are, we shall be in a position to appreciate them later on. So, I would ask him to please stay still a bit and allow those who have serious things to say to express themselves in this house.
Mr. Chairman, in his brief speech and his short statement of excuses, the Postmaster General did not touch on a side of his department's administration which is indeed one of the most important ones, since his department is supposed to be the only one able to support itself, without having to rely on any grant whatever from the federal government.

For instance, the minister has failed, unintentionally or not, to mention salary increases for certain postal employees, increases which he called for when he was but a very noisy private member and critic of the Post Office Department for the then official opposition.
He also used to deal with the improvement of working conditions in that department. In fact, all will admit that the present Postmaster General was the champion of the improvement of working conditions for the employees of the Post Office Department. He no longer talks about that now.
Mr. Chairman, a matter which seems to have haunted the Postmaster General when he was only the private member for St. Denis, is that of the thefts in post offices. In fact, I recall that he used to repeat the same story all the time, that there was not a single day when we would not have heard the hon. member for St. Denis ask the then postmaster general if he was not aware that a burglary had taken place in such and such a post office.
I was really surprised to note that the Postmaster General made no mention at all of post office thefts in his brief statement on presenting his estimates. Yet, those thefts keep on happening and are even getting more serious since the minister was appointed to his present duties.
When he analysed the situation in his department, the minister failed to suggest a policy to ensure a balanced budget. As a matter of fact, we are far from the balance policy he always advocated when he was in the opposition.
He acquired a wide experience and showed great competence since he was elected to the house, more especially since he was designated as official critic of the opposition on postal matters. At that time, he put himself to a lot of trouble. He searched through all the departmental files and he even had access to confidential reports the then postmaster general was kind enough to let him consult.
In the light of the minister's comments, we must come to the conclusion that, since he took over as Postmaster General, he has not put into practice any new formula and none of the suggestions he made when he was sitting in the opposition.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote certain observations the present Postmaster General made on July 26, 1958, when he was just the private member for St. Denis, and which show exactly the situation in which the Postmaster General finds himself once again today. The situation which the minister promoted a few years ago has become for him, today, a stumbling block, and it cannot be denied that when he was sitting in the
Supply-Post Office
opposition, the minister played a much more efficient role than he is playing today.
I should have liked the Postmaster General to speak more extensively on the question which obsessed him when he was in the opposition. I do not intend to quote all the insignificant allegations recited in the past by the present Postmaster General; neither do I intend to give an account of the debates, reflections, complaints and laments he was then heard to express. On the other hand, he spoke of thefts, as though they had been invented; he spoke about the postal system, saying the department owed it to itself to grant the country two postal deliveries a day.
I could quote the words of the member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), as reported in the official record for July 26, 1958, and so applicable to the present Postmaster General. I could not let this opportunity go by without reminding him of his own words, which, today, must leave him quite ill at ease in his present position.
Concerning thefts in post offices, I have before me a newspaper article mentioning a recent theft in Montreal, involving over $40,000. I learned through another article, a few days ago, that a post office had been robbed of about $20,000. Since the minister has been there, you learn that everywhere in this country post offices suffer important thefts. I wonder why the Postmaster General, after four years experience in the opposition, at which time he was obsessed, as I was saying a while ago, by thefts occurring in post offices, did not find it appropriate to tell us what he thought of this situation, and especially what means he intends to use to protect the valuables and other articles that the department is entrusted with.
It takes him a long time to understand.

I agree with the hon. member for Villeneuve when he says the Postmaster General takes a long time to understand.
Mr. Chairman, if we cannot discuss objectively the estimates introduced by the Postmaster General, it is because we notice that the estimates are in accordance with reality. That is what we find strange and the only explanation I could find is that they were prepared by our administration, which goes to show once again that the people had no reason to overthrow a government which had such a good record of administrating public business that the present Postmaster General adopts the same system.
Of course, the Postmaster General gave new guide lines to his department's policy, guide lines which clearly indicate the philosophy of the government now in power, because since they have taken over, the Liberals

Supply-Post Office
have applied the policy of patronage of which the Postmaster General is but one example giving us an opportunity to point out the most crucial and most shocking problems. And to think that those people were elected on the commitment to bring new life to the federal administration.
The Postmaster General specially forgot to discuss the matter of the salary increases asked for by his employees for so long. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that when we were in power, we gave a salary increase to post office employees.
I have in front of me a few letters from people who are asking how it is possible that with an administration headed by a man who promised during so many years to raise the post office staff salaries, not only the employees have not had any increase, but they had a cut in their salary. In fact, I wonder whether it is the policy of the government to consider increasing the wages of the employees.
One of my constituents wrote me on August 17 saying:
-As you undoubtedly know, the employees have been granted an increase: the workers on the fourth floor at least were given an increase of 16 cents per hour, I think, but our wages were reduced by 14 cents per hour. We were earning $1.57 and we now receive $1.43 an hour for the same work-
A policy of grandeur.

Yes, I am wondering whether this is a policy of grandeur and whether the Postmaster General is showing a genuine interest in the wages of postal workers, as he promised while he was in the opposition.
I also have a document to prove that under the Conservative administration all employees had been granted some rather substantial increases. I shall spare the house the enumeration of all those increases and all the categories of persons who benefited therefrom. In any case, I think the Postmaster General is aware of those salary increases. Nevertheless, I would have liked to hear him tell us what policy he intends to follow in this matter.
The Postmaster General knows as well as I do that the employees of his department are rendering a valuable service to society. They are dedicated people who do not count the hours spent at the service of the Post Office Department, though their health may sometimes suffer.
Since all the bills having received most careful consideration by the government were designed to raise the salary rates of high government officials in Canada-there is also the bill which enabled the members of this house to get a rather substantial increase- I wonder whether the minister could now look after the little people and at long last solve

a problem that is surely worthy of more attention than the minister has been giving to it until now.
If I am not mistaken, the minister did not refer to the steps advocated by the Glassco commission in its report on the improvement of efficiency in the postal service. Unfortunately, being a good Liberal administrator, he overlooked the recommendations of the Glassco commission. He should have realized that it would have been to the advantage of the Canadian people to apply certain steps and he could then have told us something about the improvement in service the public is asking for.
I have here an article published in La Presse of October 15, 1963, in which it is said:
-But if Mr. Denis is convinced that without those increases, there will be a deficit in his department, the public is just as convinced that, without an increase in the number of wicket clerks, at the Place d'Armes post office among others, some day there will be a fresh outbreak of separatism.
I think that if the Postmaster General would really take the trouble of considering the administrative problems for which he is responsible rather than considering the request for patronage made to him by sympathizers of the great Liberal cause, it would certainly result in some great improvement for the public.
Mr. Chairman, the minister gave us a broad outline, a little while ago. His outline of the situation was somewhat too broad to allow him to make any concrete announcement. For instance, he spoke about the pay increase granted to sub-postmasters but when I inquired about the nature of that increase, I was not surprised to learn that it was $5 a month. What a big improvement, what an acknowledgement of the services and devotion of that category of employees.
I am wondering whether the minister was in earnest when he said that owing to his personal intervention, the postmasters' salaries had been increased, while they were only increased by $60 a year. If the minister's intervention has no better result than that, I believe he could really ask his leader to recommend him for a job in which a $60 a year increase could be considered as a special treatment for him.
However, I believe the Postmaster General juggled with his department's expenditures and has not concerned himself with bringing improvements such as those made by the former government, which came to power in 1957, and that on the whole, the administration entrusted to him is a complete failure.
The present Postmaster General had been so voluble when he was a member of the

opposition that people had expected something more than the incoherent statements he has given us this afternoon.
Of course, I understand the minister is in a somewhat difficult position; rumour has it that an appointment would be intended for him in a much quieter and easier place, in a less committing position. So I believe that having in mind a promotion in another place, the minister has not taken pains to examine thoroughly the problems inherent to his department.
We are not going to blame him too much for that, because we are under the impression that the Prime Minister will know how to reward him during the Christmas holidays. And as we are in a festive spirit, I should like to take this opportunity to wish the Postmaster General to find in his Christmas stocking the appointment that he has been wishing for all these years, and the house will not be any worse off for it. Upon our return, we shall be able to offer him our warmest congratulations for getting a transfer to a world of tranquillity instead of worries, as he experiences at this time.
When the minister said earlier, that patronage had been introduced into the Post Office Department by the former administration, I had the impression that he was referring to the former Conservative administration. But after checking my material, I understood that he was referring rather to the former Liberal administration. If the minister wants to be honest and consistent, he can refresh his memory by looking into an article published in La Presse on May 31, 1951, that is close to 13 years ago, when the Conservatives were not in office. That article proves that patronage was really a Liberal creation for which the minister, in order to make excuses for himself, is trying now to blame the former Conservative administration.
That article has this to say:
Members of the opposition maintained yesterday in the Commons that appointments made in the Post Office Department are sometimes the result of patronage.
Members of the three opposition parties criticized the way appointments were made during consideration of the bill presented by the Hon. Mr. Rinfret, postmaster general, to amend and revise the legislation concerning the postal service.
Mr. Chairman, that article was published in that newspaper at a time when our friends opposite were in power. That goes to show that the minister was mistaken, once again, when he said that patronage started under the Conservative administration. It is more of a genuine Liberal system, it is part of the Liberal party's concepts and philosophy to use power to its own advantage rather than to serve the people.

If I were the only member here to make that charge, I think the hon. members opposite would be justified to question my word. But when we come back to the reason why the member for St. Denis is part of the cabinet as Postmaster General, we get the feeling of being before the Liberal party's executioner, that is to say the patronage handler in the highest sense of the word. There is no doubt that patronage came into the federal administration with the Postmaster General.
Some time ago, when we asked the Postmaster General if he had really compiled a patronage list, he stated, upon his word as a minister, that there was no patronage list in his office.
When we plied him with questions, the minister finally admitted that there was a list, but that it was not a patronage list. It was a list which he called a "list of consultants".
I regret to say that the minister misled the house when he said that there was no patronage list in his office and when he called the list a "list of consultants".
After examining that notorious list of consultants, we were in a position to see that this list, by error or for political reasons, included the names of Liberal candidates defeated in the last election, in all the ridings in Canada.
Yet, knowing the man who was my political opponent and who, by the way, did not even live in the riding, I wondered how he could have been appointed a consultant to the Post Office Department with his lack of qualifications. At least if he had been a consultant. The Postmaster General knows full well that the Quebec minimum wage act forbids employers to pay their employees less than the minimum wage. Now, I feel that those people should be paid a salary by the department, particularly if they are qualified consultants.
We made a comparison and we came to the conclusion-

-and if he is not satisfied I hope he will ask me another question. I will conclude my remarks in English because I would like the hon. member to have the opportunity of getting the meaning that I want to convey with regard to the patronage list to which he has referred.

Mr. Chairman, at the request of my friend for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner), I shall pursue my remarks in French.
When the minister was accused of having such a list, he said: "We have no patronage list." Later on, he said: "Your Conservative list was worse than ours".
When a minister states that there is no patronage list and then ends up saying "Your list was worse than ours", it seems to me that there is a lack of coherence on his part, as regards the official or non-official recognition of a list that really existed.
Now, to answer the question put to me a moment ago, I have here the list of consultants that was prepared in the minister's office-
Those are two identical lists.
He is somebody, he is a man.

A good man who almost lost his deposit, despite the speech made by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napier-ville (Mr. Dupuis) in the riding of St. Mary.
We have here, Mr. Chairman, the list of consultants issued by the Liberal party, and we find that the basic difference between the patronage list of the Liberal party and its list of consultants is that on the list the Postmaster General had in his office, in all ridings where Liberal members were defeated, Liberal candidates were appointed patronage agents under the title of consultants to the Postmaster General.
When the minister said that there was a list of Conservatives identical to his own, I say here that he misled the house, either by ignorance or knowingly, in order to clear himself.
I am in a position to prove that statement, and I can tell the hon. member that the list referred to by the minister was a list of addresses, prepared during the last electoral campaign and containing the addresses of all the Conservative candidates who had organization committees in each of the counties, and not a list of former candidates.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, I think that the hon. members opposite have misunderstood what I meant when I said that the former postmaster general had issued a list of addresses in March 1963, so that the mail addressed to the members of the House of Commons could be redirected to the various constituencies. It was not a list which was put in the office of the minister for patronage, for placing people in post offices, as is done at the present time.
I appreciate that our hon. friends might have some difficulty to see the difference; indeed, they do not want to see the difference. We are proving to them that under the Conservative administration there was no such thing as a patronage list, while under the Liberals such a list is official, classifying as "consultants" defeated candidates in the election.
That list is a sort of open sesame to the various post offices throughout Canada, whereas, under the Conservative administration, the only thing the postmaster general did, was to advise the offices that this or that member could be found at the address of a central committee during the electoral campaign. That was a normal thing to do. It was not a matter of patronage, it was a list of addresses, and I know-

speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted to him has expired.
I hope that the house will allow me a few more minutes, for we have on many occasions agreed to listen to the nonsense of certain members opposite.
Mr. Chairman, I would ask the house to agree to let the hon. member go on with his remarks, since he is far from being offensive.

I can understand the Postmaster General stating that I am not offensive, for he himself is very defensive; but he would just the same like to be in another situation.
I know that I must thank him for the opportunity he has given me to reiterate the wish which we all make, that the new year would increase, in the interest of the House of Commons, the number of senators and deliver us from his presence.
Finally, he will be regarded as one of the postmaster generals who indulged the most in patronage in the history of this country.
Mr. Chairman, the time allocated to the hon. member has now expired and I object to his continuing to talk nonsense.
This is going to be good.
Mr. Chairman, I hear the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Berger) say that this is going to be good. It will certainly be better than it is in his constituency.

Mr. Chairman, may I raise a point of order. My point of order is that it is the normal course of events to see the spokesman for the various parties recognized in the order of party precedence in the house, and therefore the hon. member for Danforth should have been recognized.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I appreciate this point. That is what I had proposed to do but I must say I did not see the hon. member for Danforth until I had called on the hon. member for Villeneuve. Perhaps the hon. member for Villeneuve may want to yield the recognition I accorded him in favour of the hon. member for Danforth.
Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure for me to follow the traditions of the house and I shall leave the floor to the hon. member for Danforth.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to thank the hon. member for Villeneuve. I had not intended to raise the matter myself, but the hon. member for Skeena is always insistent on the rules being followed and is a great respecter of the rules and traditions of the house. I thank the hon. member for Villeneuve for yielding to me.
There are a few remarks I should like to make on behalf of our party with regard to this department. I should like to begin by saying that most of them, in fact all of them, are not directed at the minister in any personal way. I have had occasion to have dealings with the minister on postal matters, and from a personal point of view I can say I have found him to be quite co-operative and very fair. I want to make that clear. I wanted to say that at the beginning, because the balance of my remarks will not be quite as congratulatory of the minister and the government.
Over the years the Post Office Department, of course, has been a department that has not always received the care and attention that is should have received from parliament and from the ministers who have looked after its affairs. From our examination it is our view that one of the best cabinet ministers ever to handle this portfolio was Mr. W. Hamilton, a former member from Montreal, I believe. An examination of the records and
Supply-Post Office
of his performance of his duties shows that he did make an honest, sincere and partially successful attempt to root out many of the more flagrant abuses. It is regrettable in a way that he was removed from our midst by the wishes of his constituents in the 1962 election, because we have never felt that his successors measured up to his ability. As I have said, the department is one which is capable of great use or great misuse. Signs already appearing, which we can see, seem to indicate that some of the older and more reprehensible practices in this department are again rearing their heads.
I was interested in the speech of the hon. member for St. Mary, much of which I thought was needlessly self-congratulatory of the previous government, and some of it quite hypocritical. The criticisms he has been making could more properly have been directed, and to some degree with greater validity, toward the administration which preceded the present one. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, one of the most depressing aspects this session is the constant refrain we hear from this side of the house that all the present government is doing is carrying on the brilliant and marvellous programs introduced by the Conservatives when they formed the government.
I want to deal with the department in two or three aspects, and the first one is one which has partially been raised by the previous speaker. I refer to patronage. We have heard a great deal about this. In fact, I notice that most members on the other side of the house have their little lists of consultants and they are waving them with great glee. I do not know how many there are in the house but it is quite a pretty sight to see all the white sheets being waved. Of course, these lists are not new. They were used by the previous government as well. I do not know to what degree they constitute patronage, but I do think there are more serious charges of patronage that can be made against the government and ones which ought to be investigated in the next session by a special committee of the house.
May I ask a question? Will the hon. member mention the particular cases?

The minister is just about two minutes ahead of me; I am just coming to that. I am not suggesting whether these charges which have been made by responsible members of the postal department are true or not. Obviously we do not have enough evidence to judge at this stage. But they have been made and to me they constitute a very grave and serious reflection upon an important aspect of the civil service. If the charges that the present government is
28902-5-387

Supply-Post Office
instituting patronage practices for political purposes are true, we have the right to know. They should be investigated, as I have said, by a special committee of the house in the next session of parliament. Obviously there is not time to do it now, and no one suggests that a serious attempt could successfully be made.
I have a photostat of an article which appeared in one of the Ottawa newspapers. In it charges are made by a Mr. Bill Houle, who is president of C.P.E.A., Montreal local. This man is not a politician but a responsible officer in his department. He has charged, at a meeting at which the deputy postmaster general, W. H. Wilson, was present-I think it was the annual dinner of the Ottawa branch which was held here-that by the use of patronage we are reintroducing patronage into the government of Canada. That is a very serious charge to make. The article does not disclose any detailed facts, but complaints were made about the manner of hiring being adopted by the department. The local postal clerk, a Mr. Bernard Belanger, asked whether the post office had a policy of hiring cheap casual help to fill jobs previously held by postal clerks, and he said that this policy would eventually result in the extinction of postal clerks. These are grave charges, Mr. Chairman. We do not know whether or not they are true, but if this trend is beginning to make itself apparent then we have the right to know about it and to try to stop it before it goes any further.
All this banter which has taken place in the house over the subject of the lists is not that important. I think it is an unpleasant thing to do and that it is somewhat improper, but I think all the hullaballoo made about it is a little silly. But we as members of parliament should be concerned at the more serious aspects of the matter which are rearing their heads. While the post office department has always been lightly regarded by the government, it is a department of some importance touching the lives of everyone in Canada, and should be looked after carefully by us in our deliberations. Therefore I suggest to the minister that he agree to have these charges investigated, and that we be permitted to call before us various individuals who have made such charges so as to ascertain whether or not they are true. It may be they are untrue. If that is the case then we should know this as well.
The other matter about which I wanted to speak is also of great importance and concerns the working conditions under which postal employees operate. We always hear a lot about the need for good postal services, for two or three deliveries a day, and taking care of the desires of the public. But I want

to make an appeal to the minister to become the champion of the postal employees, because they are the neglected part of the Post Office Department. It is all very well to talk of pretty stamps, of an annual stamp day, of a stamp for this person and a stamp for that person. But the minister would make a greater contribution to his department if he became the spokesman of, and the champion for, the rights of the employees.
I should like to put on the record something of the conditions under which they work. I think it is reprehensible that this large body of public servants should have no collective bargaining rights and no arbitration rights. We give these to all sections of the working community through our labour laws. We give them to such people as a matter of right. We give the right to our workmen to associate together and to bargain collectively for the betterment of their working conditions. Our farmers have certain farm organizations to take care of their interests. I think it is extremely reprehensible that our employees in the postal department do not have similar rights.
I think most members received a bulletin from the federated association of letter carriers in June of this year headed: "The Postmen ask, is it fair". In this bulletin are set out some of the onerous conditions under which these people are working, and I should like to put them on record.
The letter carrier Is made completely responsible for the mail on his route. He has personal and individual responsibility as compared to the average postal employee who works in a group.
He is responsible for registered mail and for all changes of address, sometimes for as long as a year, sometimes indefinitely. He re-addresses all changes and keeps an up to date directory for this purpose, and notifies publishers of changes in address.
In addition he has recently been assigned the task of redirecting family allowance and old age pension cheques, formerly a responsibility of the recipients.
He is responsible for collecting government money through C.O.D. items, short-paid mail and custom and excise charges.
He must personally investigate complaints that mail which was posted was not delivered, often due to the fault of others, and write an explanation on a special enquiry form.
In dealing with the public he is expected to do a good "public relations" job for the government and the post office in particular. He is expected to be neat in appearance, courteous and knowledgeable.
He is expected to carry ever-increasing loads. In a ten year period the average walk has increased by more than 100 calls and 400 pieces of mail daily.
Despite advancing age he is expected to keep in top physical condition in order to perform his job quickly and efficiently. He must stick on the job until his daily task is completed. While he has a starting hour he has no finishing time.

The carrier is up and on the job by at least 6.30 a.m., often earlier.
Apart from a ten minute coffee break he has to go without lunch until his last item of mail is delivered. This can be a six-hour grind and often is even longer.
He must carry out his duties in all kinds of weather, outdoors all year round, in temperatures from the nineties to below zero, through rain and snow and upon treacherous, icy sidewalks and stairs.
Aside from regular mail he is the pack-horse for business firms who load his walk with bundles of "householder" pamphlets, dodgers and other sales promotion literature, which he must deliver to every letter box on his route-a veritable gold mine for the post office in the Toronto area alone.
While other postal workers are required to work many hours overtime the carrier is expected to prepare and deliver his volume in a regular working day.
Working under these wonderful conditions, Mr. Chairman, the letter carrier has had no pay increase in almost three years. His average weekly wage is $67.50 take home pay; that is a man with two children. The bulletin continues:
Many wives and mothers must work to make ends meet and many carriers take second jobs to support their families. Like the low man on the totem pole he carries the great weight of those above him and receives the least attention for his efforts. Is it any wonder the letter carriers ask: Is it fair?
These kind of working conditions would not be tolerated by this government.
I was at the reception the other day for the Canadian Labour Congress and I never saw a more smoothly managed stage performance or such a degree of interest in labour. Labour is going to get anything it wants. I have never seen such interest in the working man. He is going to get a fair deal. They could not have been more careful in the way they were currying favour. But in the department over which the minister has control there are people working under these types of conditions, who have no collective bargaining rights, for which they have been asking for years. They have been asking for compulsory arbitration so that they can force upon an unwilling government the awards which an arbitrator would give them, and they cannot get that right either. I appeal to the minister, as I said at the start of this phase of my remarks. If he wants to be a great minister and to elevate himself above the level at which most postmasters have been content to serve, then let him become the champion of the people in his department. From letters I have received I am under the impression that morale in the Post Office Department is low. I hope I am wrong in this. But I suggest to the hon. gentleman that he should get out of his office and talk to some of the people who work in his department. Never mind the senior officials, though they are perfectly 28902-5-3874
Supply-Post Office
competent. The minister should find out what are the feelings of the letter carriers and of the workers in some of the lower levels in the post office. These people are unhappy. They feel that no one really cares about their working conditions. I do not think this state of affairs will be improved until the minister himself is ready to get out into the field and find out the thoughts and wishes of those who work there. If he were to do that, there would be at least a chance of bringing about an improvement in conditions.
Some consideration should be given to establishing a fairer method of handling dismissals. At the present time, employees who are dismissed are entitled to appeal to a higher body. Some of us have had occasion to appear before these kangaroo courts. They are loaded in favour of the department. The applicant rarely has an opportunity to call witnesses, or else he finds witnesses are not available. I appeared before such a body on behalf of one employee and I sent in a list of the people I wanted to call as witnesses in support of my case. They were astonished. This had never been done. They were all working. They were not available. Consequently, there was no evidence to repudiate the charges which were made and in due course a notice came out to say that the appeal had been dismissed. I have never appeared before a more one-sided kangaroo court. I should like to see the minister do something to remedy this state of affairs and give employees a better chance. In particular he should make sure that those who come down from Ottawa to hear these cases have all the evidence before them. I do not criticize them. If they do not hear both sides of the case they cannot make an intelligent judgment. But by controlling the evidence to which the board has access the department is, in effect, controlling the decisions. I think this is a situation which should be changed.
The minister should give consideration to increasing the remuneration paid to the thousands of people who operate sub-post offices. I spent the whole summer in my constituency trying to get a new sub-post office established. I did not think of going to see the consultant. I might have got some action if I had had the forethought to do that, but it did not occur to me at the time. The real difficulty we encountered was that no one would take on the job. We found all kinds of individuals who are interested in running a post office, but as soon as I quoted the rates they politely showed me the door. The rates are so low that it is not worth the trouble of providing a service. This is not an effective way in which to operate the department. I ask the minister to give serious thought to this, because the present rates of

Supply-Post Office
remuneration are affecting the quality of the service from coast to coast, and I think they are affecting the quality of the individuals who serve in our sub-post offices.
I do not wish to continue at any great length because I know there are a great many speakers to follow me and they will probably cover the subjects which I omit. I should like to conclude by renewing my appeal to the minister. I know there are rumours in the newspapers that he is not going to be here very long. I hope they are not true. I hope he will stay with us and that he will find within himself the qualities necessary to make this department a much better department than it is at the present time. There are areas which are in grave need of overhaul. Some of this work was started by Mr, Hamilton when he was postmaster general but I do not think any serious attempt has been made since that time. One of our disappointments so far is that the present minister does not give us on this side of the house the impression that he intends to use the qualities he possesses. We do not get the impression that the minister really understands the problems of this department or that he is the type of minister who would turn his whole party against him, if necessary. 1 am told that Mr. Hamilton was such a good postmaster that he did not have a single friend in the Tory party. I do not want to interfere with the hon. gentleman's friendships but if he were able to announce next year that he was so good, so impartial, so anxious to serve the needs of the post office at the expense of his party that he did not have a single, solitary friend in the Liberal party, this would be the greatest tribute he could be paid.

I wish to make only a few remarks with respect to the estimates of the Post Office Department which are before us now. At the outset I think it was well known in this house to the dismay of most members that we see this ugly trend toward patronage coming up again in a government department. It seems it has shown up more in the Post Office Department because of lists which have been tabled and if there are such things in other departments, we do not know they are there but we hope they are not.
The fact is that members have these lists before them now and they are extremely sorry that this kind of thing is being continued. In my opinion, in this enlightened age when we have technological apparatus available to us and to the leaders of parties, and to members and candidates, to communicate with the mass of the people in Canada, in their constituencies in particular, this kind of patronage which has begun to show up again is, in fact, a liability to a political party, rather than an

asset. I know that in days gone by when there were no facilities for mass communication with the people there were politicians and political party organizers in various areas who were consultants, and so on. It may have been a political asset then, but I am certain that in the long range view today any form of patronage of the nature that is showing up now is, in fact, a liability. It belongs to an age that has gone past and I certainly hope we are going to see an end to it, particularly in the post office.
I was interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for St. Mary. If I understood him correctly-and he was interrupted a few times-he said the purpose of the lists which were tabled was to enable the department to find members of parliament after the election. If he did not say that, I apologize. But if he did say something to that effect I would like to pose a question. I read from the front page of this list, sessional paper 255, part I, and it says:
Effective immediately. All matters pertaining to Newfoundland will be referred to James A. McGrath, M.P. and I think at the time of referral he should be supplied with the name and address of the individual who is our normal consultant concerned with the particular problems.
What does that mean? Does that mean you needed the list so you could forward mail and, furthermore, what do they mean by "all matters pertaining to Newfoundland-"

Since the hon. member asked me a question, I would like to refer him to the dates on this list, which are February 8, February 26 and March 26. It was, in fact, a demand from members of parliament so that their addresses should be changed in order that their mail would be forwarded to them during the campaign. There is nothing connected with patronage about this. It is just a list so that the mail will reach members of parliament.

I see there is an amendment no. 11, dated March 6, 1963. I see that very plainly. On the face of it, it says "effective immediately on all matters." "All matters" must include more than having addresses. I think the hon. member would consider me naive indeed if I were to conclude these were only lists of addresses.
I have in my hand the Conservative list, by the way, and I notice that in Medicine Hat the consultant to the Postmaster General is Edwin W. Brunsden, care of Progressive Conservative campaign headquarters, South Railway street, Medicine Hat. He is to be addressed as "Dear Ted". The evidence is fairly clear, Mr. Chairman. Let us look at the Liberal list. I find that in Medicine Hat the consultant is to be Dave Broadfoot, of Redcliff, Alberta. For the benefit of hon.

members who do not already know, I may say that Dave Broadfoot was the Liberal candidate who ran against me. In Edmonton-Strathcona, the name of the consultant is John Decore. In Edmonton West, the consultant is J. Harper Prowse. He was also a defeated Liberal candidate. In the constituency of Lethbridge, the one right next to mine, the consultant is Martin Hoyt. He also was a defeated Liberal candidate.
I would ask the Postmaster General what it is about which he consults these gentlemen? Are they experts in the administration of the post office? Do they have some special knowledge about where post office buildings should be put? Do they have some knowledge of the general administration of a post office, or just what is the reason for having them on the list, and what kind of questions do you refer to them for their counsel? This is an important bit of information, Mr. Chairman. What kind of questions have been referred? So far as I am concerned, I do not know that any of these gentlemen in the constituencies about which I have information, have any special knowledge that would be important to the Postmaster General in the operations of the Post Office Department.
As a matter of fact, the results of the elections would seem to indicate these gentlemen did not even have a high degree of public support. They were not only defeated, but they were away down the list in being defeated. As I have said, Mr. Chairman, this kind of operation belongs to an age long past. The Liberal government and the Postmaster General in particular would be well advised to recognize that we have moved out of that era where this political patronage was an asset to a political party.
During the election campaign of 1957, and for a number of years prior to that, the Liberal candidate of that time used a great deal of his time, and in fact most of his campaign was based on being present at the opening of post offices and federal buildings throughout the constituency. He had no hesitation about making it evident that, as Liberal candidate, he got in touch with the Liberal government of that day and that credit should be given to him for getting the building. This was true of places like Taber, Brooks, and others about which I know. He was at the official opening and made it abundantly clear he was instrumental in seeing that the people got these buildings.
I want the Postmaster General-I see the Minister of Public Works is here too-to know that the electorate in the constituency resented it, rather than giving him credit for it. This pursuit of political patronage was not an asset but was a liability. I am not suggesting to the Minister of Public Works that
Supply-Post Office
this sort of thing is going on now. I am just telling him what happened at that time. Even at that time, this kind of patronage was a liability rather than an asset. The candidate's vote went down substantially after he engaged in this kind of activity.
I do not want to take a lot more time of the committee, Mr. Chairman. We have these lists. I hope the Postmaster General will resolve now that he is going to destroy these lists and use the officials within his department who are supposed to have some knowledge of the administration of the department when he needs advice. I can understand the frustration of some of the officials, the regional officials of the Post Office Department, when they try to do something on the basis of what is right and what is in keeping with good administration, only to be overridden roughshod by some political consultant who may not agree with what they are trying to do.
A political hack.

Hack is the word. I say in all kindness to the Postmaster General that if he can get himself to change his attitude towards this political patronage and recognize that this is nearly 1964 and this kind of patronage is no longer any good, even for practical politics, then perhaps we can have good, solid administration of the Post Office Department. On the other hand, if he intends to pursue this business in the way he has, and in the way it has been done by almost all federal governments in the past, then I think we should have an investigation into the department. I think, too, that if he persists in pursuing this kind of administration, perhaps Canada would be better off if we had a different Postmaster General.

Mr. Chairman, we are considering at present the estimates of a fairly important department, namely the Post Office Department, and the minister in charge is well-known to me since we were colleagues from 1946 to 1949. At that time, the Postmaster General (Mr. Denis) was a member of the famous "Little Chicago" sitting to the right of the Speaker, at this end of the chamber. The present premier of Quebec also belonged to that group.
We are happy to see that the minister has matured intellectually since then. At least, he seems to take his office seriously and I am happy to see him at the head of such an important department.
Mr. Chairman, there are only 15 items for this department; the estimates amount to $191,166,000 and the number of postal workers is 56,371.

Supply-Post Office
Mr. Chairman, one has to agree that 15 items are not too many tor such an important department. As a matter of fact, this reminds somewhat of the story to the guy who asked for a bowl of pea soup in a restaurant. When the soup was served to him, he noticed that there were only three peas in his plate. He called the owner of the place and asked him: "Tell me, where do you buy those peas?" The owner said: "Why do you ask?" And the man replied: "I never saw three peas that made so much juice."
As tor me, Mr. Chairman, I never saw 15 items involving so many expenditures. It is indeed a remarkable thing.
Mr. Chairman, the previous speakers have mentioned the high degree of patronage dispensed in the Post Office Department. I will not accuse the minister himself of dispensing patronage, but I will surely blame the system and those who allow this system to be maintained not only within the Post Office Department but also in others.
As for the Post Office Department, I have already called the attention of the minister on the patronage dispensed in my constituency and after having asked a copy of the correspondence exchanged between an employee of the Post Office Department and my constituents, I received copy of letters from the employment division, the contract assessment and tenders division of the Post Office Department.
Mr. Chairman, I have here the correspondence exchanged since the month of May, that is since this government came into office, and October 25 last, that is less than a month and a half ago, between the department and Mr. Stephen Cuddihy, ex-Liberal candidate defeated by more than 11,000 votes on April 8 last.
Mr. Stephen Cuddihy is a young lawyer aged 26 or 27, who knows absolutely nothing about postal administration. And now the high officials of the postal department write to him to advise him that the appointment of Mr. Hector Villeneuve as postmaster at Rapide Sept was confirmed on October 25, 1963. What does a Rouyn lawyer care about the appointment of Mr. Villeneuve as postmaster? And that letter is signed by Mr. DeGaspe Tache, acting director of personnel.
If Mr. A. DeGaspe Tache, high official at the Post Office Department, is not aware yet of the fact that Real Caouette is the member for the riding of Villeneuve, I take it upon myself to let him know. I will also draw his attention to the fact that all federal hon. members, whether they are from the New Democratic, the Conservative or the Social Credit parties, are entitled to know what is going on in their riding, and that even if high officials of the department are con-

cerned, whether it is Mr. A. DeGaspe Tache or Mr. R. A. Cathro, director of transport- whatever the names are-this sort of patronage must stop.
The people in my riding pay taxes to the federal government as much as the voters in the Postmaster General's riding, and the onus does not lie upon the high officials of the Post Office Department to decide who must pull the wires in a riding, on behalf of a political party, whatever it is. We must be more respectful of the principles of democracy, if we boast of living in a democratic country, because a democratic country is ruled by a government of the people, elected by the people and for the people. We must show some respect at least to those who are elected by the people.
On September 25, 1963, Mr. R. A. Cathro writes once again to Mr. Stephen Cuddihy:
Mr. Sylvio Pilotte, postal contractor on rural route No. 1, Val Senneville, has requested a salary increase.
Following a complete review, it has been established that $1,750 would be a fair salary for the work involved. This would represent a yearly increase of $175.
Consequently, the department intends to increase Mr. Pilotte's salary from $1,575 to $1,750 a year, as from October 1, 1963.
Yours truly,
R. A. Cathro Director of Transport
What does that matter to Stephen Cuddihy?
What has he got to do with that?
What has notary Morin of Val d'Or got to do in the management of the postal service?
But it goes even further, and I continue. I shall not quote all the letters, but I have one dated September 23, 1963, from Mr. DeGaspe Tache to Mr. Stephen Cuddihy, another dated September 9, 1963, from Mr. Cathro to Mr. Stephen Cuddihy, the latter concerning Mr. Ulysse Charette, of Sullivan, stating that his salary will be increased by $205.64 a year.
I have another letter written by Mr. Cathro to Mr. Cuddihy, on May 31, 1963. It is strange that Mr. Cathro never wrote me to ask for information or to make suggestions to me about the riding of Villeneuve.
Because he was never asked for that.

He was never asked for that.
I have a still better one, dated September 5, 1963:
Mr. Stephen Cuddihy 90 Perreault East Rouyn, P.Q.
Dear Sir,
On August 24, 1963, we had to close down sub-office No. 1 which was situated at 607 Murdoch (Blue Sundries), because Mrs. Cotnoir, the postmistress, sold her store.

That small office was well situated to accommodate patrons from the western part of town who, mostly, must travel one mile to go to the main post office.
Those far-away patrons miss their small post office and make it clear to us in no uncertain terms and in the most democratic way, by circulating a petition on which we have about 90 names.
Mr. Cuddihy, I ask you to try and do something for them. I shall be pleased to open a new post office when I have the authorization.
If you require further information, do not hesitate to contact the undersigned.
J. C. I.anglois Postmaster Noranda, P.Q.
The very person who gave tender forms to Mr. Cuddihy last fall for the repainting of mailboxes in the limits of Noranda. You remember that he gave him three tender forms and said to him: hand these to your friends and manage so that the one who deserves a favour from the government gets the contract. Things happened that way and those tender forms were presented to a garageman in Rouyn, his manager and his first salesman, who were asked to submit a tender at the Noranda post office, to Mr. Langlois.
Mr. Chairman, such behaviour should be stigmatized and those who put such methods into practice should be held up to public scorn. That is what I am doing at the present time in this house.
I am not surprised that the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) does not understand those words, as he never understands anything.
Mr. Chairman, on September 3, 1963, Mr. Cathro wrote to Mr. Theo Beaudry and to Mr. Stephen Cuddihy, two former Liberal candidates:
Service: Louvicourt and Senneterre, contractor: Narcisse Grand'Maison, price:	$3,588.80 a year,
expiring date: December 31, 1963.
The contract in connection with the above-mentioned service expires on the specified date.
The department is ready to renew the contract at the present rate of payment, for another period of four years.
For four years, without calling tenders, at the request of former Liberal candidates from Chapleau and from Villeneuve.
The list goes on. On August 30, 1963, Mr. Cathro writes again to Mr. Stephen Cuddihy in connection with Duparquet.
On August 15, 1963, Mr. Cathro wrote to Mr. Stephen Cuddihy:
Service: Rouyn and La Sarre H.S., contractor: Mr. Rene Marchand.
The department accepts once more to renew the contract as of December 31, 1963.
On June 28, 1963, Mr. Cathro writes to Mr. Cuddihy:
Supply-Post Office
Service: Amos and Val d'Or, contractor: Abitibl Provincial Inc., price: $1,983.63 a year, expiring date: September 30, 1963.
-The department would be willing to renew the contract at the present rate for a further period of four years-
On June 10, 1963, Mr. Cathro sent another letter to Stephen Cuddihy:
Service: Val d'Or, R.R. No. 1, contractor: G. Henri Tremblay, price: $1,550. a year.
Expiring date: September 30, 1965-
In that case, the department is again willing to renew the contract.
This is what Mr. Cathro wrote to Mr. Stephen Cuddihy on June 3, 1963:
Service:	Val d'Or and parcel post delivery,
contractor: Mrs. J. Rousseau-Rivard, 856 Fourth avenue, Val d'Or, Que., price: 10 cents per item-
I should like to draw the minister's attention to the price of 10 cents an item which is paid to those who handle parcel post delivery to residences and places of business. In my opinion, that is not enough. The price paid is far from being sufficient since the contractors get into debt, especially in a district like ours where the climate is fairly harsh.
Along the same lines, the department pays only $1,150 for mail transportation to settlements like Mont Brun. That is not enough; the price should be raised by $200 at least.
Mr. Chairman, a few minutes ago, we were talking about two lists of consultants, that of the Conservatives and that of the Liberals. The Liberal consultant in the riding of Villeneuve is Stephen Cuddihy. There is no mistake about that since his name appears on the list which also states that the member of parliament is Real Caouette who may be addressed familiarly in all correspondence. That is the close relationship I have with the minister-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Quite an honour.

Indeed.
Mr. Chairman, the list of consultants is obviously a patronage list. Furthermore, I would say that there is no difference in that respect between the Conservatives and the Liberals. The former did exactly the same thing as the present government. Thus, last year, the consultant in the riding of Villeneuve was Mr. Cloutier, a former Conservative candidate. The Conservatives wrote letters and acted just like the Liberals are doing now.
Mr. Chairman, we can understand members having personal friends in their constituency. However, we do not believe the Canadian people should pay the costs for political patronage. That a well-known man should be favoured instead of another one, prices being equal, there is nothing to say

Supply-Post Office
against that. But there are lots of small contracts, of small jobs, which are authorized without public tenders. That is where, it appears, political patronage is practised to the greatest extent.
If we make the total, we find that tremendous amounts are spent to the advantage of friends of the government. I do not say the Liberals only practise that policy, for the Conservatives did exactly the same thing. Besides, the estimates of the Post Office Department we are discussing-the Postmaster General mentioned that in his opening remarks-were not prepared by the present government, but by the former government, that is by the Conservatives. Those are the estimates we are asked to pass today.
When the Conservatives attack the Liberals, after having done exactly the same thing, I do not believe very much in their sincerity.
A while ago the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade) tried to explain the difference between the list of the Liberals and that of the Conservatives. In fact, he blundered thoroughly and his explanations did not stand to reason. We had proof of political patronage during the Conservative administration, as we have, today, under the Liberal government, with letters from the Post Office Department providing for the distribution, for instance, of mail contracts and the openings of post offices through the representative of the party in office in the constituencies concerned.
Mr. Chairman, I strongly object to such a way of doing things in our counties. We have not been elected to parliament to play politics, we have been elected to represent our respective electors, whether they voted Liberal, Conservative, Social Credit or New Democratic party.
Mr. Chairman, those people are worthy of respect and I think the fairest procedure for any department is to keep the member of parliament aware of what is going on in his constituency, of the projects which are to be carried out. Then, we could boast that we have democracy.
But if the government has the right to select his supporters and ignore the opposition parties, I wonder what difference there is between being red in Ottawa and red in Moscow-
Oh, oh.

-where no one has the right to live, nor to give his opinion and where opposition is not tolerated.
The government has the responsibility to respect the basic principles of democracy.

Those principles consist in respecting those who were duly and legally chosen by their electors.
Those are the observations I had to make and the suggestions I wanted to offer to the Postmaster General whom I have known for many years.
I know he is a Liberal through and through who flaunts the colour he represents, but he is also a gentleman and as I said at the beginning of my remarks, I never try to attack men as men, but rather to criticize systems.
I understand that we cannot reach perfection, neither with the present Postmaster General nor with those who will succeed or have preceded him, but one must try for perfection so as to reach a higher level, to come to a better understanding and a greater mutual respect.
In closing I will say that we are prepared to vote the estimates of the Post Office Department and that we are prepared to state, if other parties agree that there be no more speakers-in order to speed up the adoption of those estimates-we, in this corner of the house, will not have any other speaker this afternoon.
However, if others are to rise, then we will follow suit. On the other hand, we are ready to co-operate so as to vote those estimates as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
