Mr. Chairman, although I appreciate the offer just made by the hon. member for Villeneuve and assure him through you, sir, that I will be extremely brief, I feel it is my duty to mention a few points at this stage of the minister's presentation. I must say at once that I have a very high regard for the officials of the Post Office Department, the people who do the work of the department in all its various branches. They have been extremely courteous so far as I am concerned and I feel this cannot, at this particular time, go unnoticed or unmentioned.
In referring to the speakers who have preceded me, Mr. Chairman, I should mention this particular point. I do not think too many of us in the house doubt for one moment that degrees of patronage are probably practised in any government. It is not the existence of the minister's list, that I had the privilege of producing, that I disagree with, although I am opposed to such practices and I do not care who carries them out. What I am opposed to, and what I object to, is the way the minister misled this house. We can think of cases in other countries where ministers of the crown have resigned for this sort of thing. Recently in Great Britain, for example, for statements that I would say

were of no greater consequence or significance, the minister in question was not forced to resign-although perhaps he was forced to resign-but resigned of his own choosing. If we go back to the days of Hugh Dalton we recall that that minister resigned of his own accord. There are other similar situations, of course.
The point is that it is a matter of principle. If the principle cannot be upheld by the members of this chamber, then it is high time that the people took a good look at those occupying the treasury benches. In my estimation the matter was so serious that at the time the situation arose I requested that the minister resign his seat. This did not happen, of course. The Prime Minister did not see fit to remove him either. Therefore the Prime Minister must also take responsibility for this particular incident.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Danforth. He made many points in his address which I thought were fair and well directed. I will not reiterate them, but in my opinion he made some very fair suggestions in his remarks. Along the lines of what the hon. member had to say there is the matter of consideration for people in contract post offices, not only with regard to the standard of remuneration they receive for their premises and their efforts, but also from the point of view that it is high time we gave some consideration to some method of giving them a holiday period each year, whether it be a week or two weeks. I believe this matter deserves consideration.
The hon. member for Danforth also referred to discrimination within the department. I too believe this exists. I could give examples at length but I will only mention two cases. I had more reason for criticizing the minister, on the occasion of the production of the list, than that particular incident. The case I am about to refer to caused me much greater anguish. I would ask him to note the date. On April 9 of this year in one of the areas in my constituency a lady who occupied the position of junior clerk was relieved of her position, because of a situation that existed in her family the day before, with regard to certain efforts put forth in the conduct of the election on that day. I might say that in this case political patronage more or less backfired. She was engaged by the Grits in 1955, and because her husband was out of work he was given a very minor task on April 8 which resulted in the action taken in regard to her on April 9. The fact is that when I complained about the situation she was re-engaged.
However, not too many weeks passed before the position was made vacant again,
Supply-Post Office
and the job was transferred for listing under the civil service commission. I have no objection at all to the job being put under the civil service commission, but with this qualification: If it is the function of the Post Office Department to practise patronage and eliminate people who have a good history of service to the people of Canada in the department, then it is high time something were done, not so much in the department, but with regard to the minister himself; because I feel that is where the direction came from.
I also have a letter dated December 15 from the city or town, whichever category it enjoys, of Oakville. It is from a Canadian citizen and in his letter he refers to the situation in that post office by saying that it is the most disdainful thing that has happened in that community in the writer's memory. He states that Miss Jean Duncan worked in the government post office for nearly 20 years, that she was fired last July, and that she is a very capable and friendly coloured girl. He states it is the unanimous opinion of everyone to whom he had spoken regarding the matter that it is racial discrimination at its very worst. Although this despicable event took place last July the writer only learned of it recently, but hopes something can be done. He says he wrote to-and here I shall say "the Liberal member" so as not to involve him directly, who replied that he could do absolutely nothing.
I suggest to the minister that this case deserves a little consideration as well. There is one other point I should like to make before I resume my seat having to do with the statement of the minister regarding new issues of stamps next year. I wonder whether the minister has considered issuing a stamp, as recommended by the Royal Canadian Legion, to commemorate Remembrance day. The minister described some of the stamps to be issued and the occasions involved, and I believe this is one that the minister should consider. I would expect that representations have probably been made to him. If not, I make this request on behalf of this organization at this time. Before I resume my seat I should like to wish the minister well in his department and say to him "bon voyage".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am only going to speak for a very few minutes in order to comment on some of the remarks that have been made in the house this afternoon. In the short time I have been a member of the house, a little over a year, I cannot recall any other occasion when there has been such hypocrisy as was practised in the house this

Supply-Post Office
afternoon. We have heard from all the statesmen this afternoon. We have heard the hon. member for St. Mary talk about the deplorable practice of patronage. We have also heard the hon. member for Danforth and the hon. member for Villeneuve speak in similar vein, all of them members of such sterling character that they would resist the common temptations to which we all succumb now and then. We have also heard from the hon. member for Grey-Bruce-
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: -and I imagine we are going to hear from-
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the hon. member rising on a question of privilege?

I should say a point of order. I am sure the hon. member has made a slip of the tongue when he has referred to the hypocrisy of certain members this afternoon. I do not think this is quite parliamentary. I should like him to revise that word because if he wants to talk about hypocrisy I will reply to him quickly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the only comment I wish to make is that I could understand such an objection coming from other members of the house, but after the personal abuse and vindictiveness this particular member heaped upon the Postmaster General not more than three quarters of an hour ago it seems very strange that he should raise a question of privilege at this time. However, to save the time of the house I am quite prepared to change "hypocrisy" to "exercise in insincerity" if that will please the hon. member any better.
It may not be better, but it is parliamentary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: I suppose we are going to hear the issue of patronage ragged to death for the rest of the afternoon. In my opinion this involves a greater waste of time, so far as the taxpayers are concerned, than the picayune patronage in lists like these. I will be the first to concede also that waving these lists, on which the name of practically every member of the house is to be found, outside of the minority parties, is also a complete waste of time.
Our hands are clean.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
I would be the last to defend patronage. I think that the situation certainly calls for a review. It may be that so far as
[Mr. Munro.1
our own party and the official opposition are concerned the issue of patronage should be resolved by deciding to do away with it. But until it is resolved it certainly seems strange that it should be laid at the doorstep of one particular cabinet minister and that he should be pilloried when all of us, except those in the minority parties, have participated in this practice in years gone by.
Therefore I hope that for the rest of the afternoon we can be spared hearing the saints talk about the terrible evils of patronage as it has been practised in the Post Office Department. Some of my friends in the official opposition have been here longer than I have and they will know how many letters one gets in a year, from the Postmaster General. As far as I am concerned, I do not believe we get very many, and they usually have to do with a postal station in one's area that probably pays so little you cannot find anybody to take the job anyway. Therefore I do not see why such an issue should be made of this matter. In many cases it is probably an assumption by a particular member of a duty which removes a headache from the department itself. But I do think the sooner we remove this practice the better. But when week after week members of the house, many of whom have been involved in this process and whose names appear on the list, get up and talk about patronage and its evils, and suggest it is confined to one party,
Sit down then.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
The hon. member for Villeneuve is one of the members of a minority party which I cannot be convinced would be so superior that any administration he headed would be absolutely pure.
I should like to comment also on what I consider a rather unfair criticism, although the hon. member for Danforth had many constructive remarks to make. He was one of the few hon. members who did have constructive remarks to make. He referred to the question of collective bargaining rights and binding arbitration for postal employees. I stand to be corrected, but as far as I am aware this is a civil service matter. Certainly it is not an issue which can be laid at the doorstep of one cabinet minister rather than at the doorstep of the government as a whole. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked the Prime Minister a short time ago about the plank in our party's platform for the 1962 and 1963 elections with regard to collective bargaining rights and binding arbitration for civil servants. The Prime Minister indicated then that we were committed to the proposal and would bring it down in due course. We have been in office about

eight or nine months, so I think it is reasonable to allow the Prime Minister and the Liberal party to bring down this legislation sooner or later, instead of criticizing the minister of one particular department. This whole exercise about post office patronage reminds me of some of our more insincere members of the house. One hon. member receives quite a bit of publicity in connection with post office patronage and starts a bandwagon rolling. Then all of a sudden we find many in the house want to get on the bandwagon, too. The bandwagon is getting a little overcrowded and I think we are all beginning to look a little ridiculous. I hope the rest of the remarks which are to follow deal with some of the more pertinent aspects of the administration of the Post Office Department, rather than being continually surfeited with sanctimonious speeches about patronage.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief. I do not agree with the hon. member who spoke last, because I feel that if we take up the time of the committee discussing patronage in the post office, or in any other department, and if as a result of that discussion that practice is eliminated, then I think we have accomplished a great deal.
Why did you not abolish it when you were in power, then?

I do not care when the practice grew up. If it grew up in 1867 I think it is still a bad practice, and that has always been my position. If the Postmaster General looks at his department's files he will discover that I expressed the view on previous occasions that where public goods and services are involved every Canadian should be given the opportunity to tender for a contract. That was the practice followed in my constituency, and it has been followed since 1957. Not a contract went out without a bid being called for publicly, giving everyone the opportunity to bid regardless of what his politics were; and the lowest bidder got the contract. I did not speak on the estimates of the Minister of Public Works last night, but if he looks at his files I am sure he will find representations made by me to the same effect. If the Postmaster General would follow that practice we would not find instances, which I will describe briefly this evening, which are again arising in my constituency. As they arise in my constituency I am sure they also arise elsewhere. I am referring to instances where there has been a departure from the fair procedure of calling for these contracts by public tender.
I mentioned to the minister the other day the opening of the new post office at Ross
Supply-Post Office
River. I suggested to him that there was an instance where, instead of advertising for bids for the performance of this service, a selective procedure was adopted whereby only a certain carrier or carriers were asked to bid. The Postmaster General said at that time that he would look into it, and I hope that if he caught the matter before the contract was actually awarded he will have been able to revise the procedure and call for public tenders on that particular contract.
There have been other instances. In his opening remarks the Postmaster General said there was not one single breach of the Post Office Act in the administration of his department since he took over as Postmaster General. The Post Office Act, if it authorizes the procedures which I have described and will be describing in a moment or two, is nothing more or less than legalized patronage, which I think is wrong. If the Post Office Act is to blame, then it should be changed.
I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the sessional papers which were tabled in reply to a motion which I had put on the order paper, I believe No. 1,170, for all copies of correspondence between the post office department and the officials thereof, and Mr. Wylie and others in Whitehorse. In the correspondence tabled was a letter from the director of transportation dated October 24, 1963. This letter concerns a contract for the carrying of mail from Dawson Creek and Whitehorse. The total cost of the contract is not a trifling sum, as indicated by the hon. member who has just taken his seat; the total amount involved is $76,630 per year. I know that the Post Office Act authorizes the minister to renew a contract which expires after three or four years, but I want to make it clear that the procedure adopted in the Yukon, which I think should be adopted nationally, is that when those contracts expire new tenders should be called. Because in every case during the six years when the Conservative party were on the government side, when these contracts were called the government got the services for a cheaper price than the going rate at the time. With one single exception every one of these contracts was put out to public tender on expiration of the contract. The exception was a case in which I made representation on behalf of a Mr. George Simmons, because he happened to be the brother of the Liberal candidate who ran against me in 1957, and I did not want him to think that I had exercised a prerogative as a member of parliament to do him out of a contract just because he happened to be on the other side of the fence. If the minister examines the records he will find that when that contract

Supply-Post Office
did go out to public tender at the next expiration date the savings to the government were almost $4,000 per annum, and the incumbent, Mr. George Simmons, was the twelfth highest bidder. In other words, he was the highest bidder of the 12 who submitted bids, and the contract was let for something over $9,000 compared with well over $12,000 previously.
This $76,630 contract expires on March 31, 1964. The letter reads as follows:
The contract for this service expires on the date indicated.
That is, in March, 1964, so there is still time to do something about it.
The department proposes to issue instructions authorizing the renewal of the contract at the existing rate for a further period of four years.
That, I say, is wrong. Tenders should be called. There are other trucking companies on the highway which can compete with the existing holder of this contract and the minister will probably find that a saving to the taxpayer would result. The letter of the director of transportation goes on to say:
As this service operates in the electoral districts of Cariboo and Yukon, a copy of this letter is being sent to persons consulted for these constituencies.
I hope that these consultants, if they have any sense of fair play at all, will advise the minister that the fairest thing to do would be to call for public tenders so that all interested Canadians having transportation facilities on the Alaska highway may have an opportunity to bid on this contract.
There is another contract which expired on September 30, 1963. This contract, says the director of transportation in a letter of May 15, 1963, to Mr. Wylie in Whitehorse, expires on the day indicated, that is, on September 30, 1963. The amount of the contract is $8,954 per annum. Here is the rest of the letter:
The department proposes to issue instructions authorizing the renewal of the contract at the existing rate for a further period of four years.
Again, let me say the minister would probably save the Canadian taxpayer money if he were to send the contract out for public tender. Even more important is the question of principle. The guiding principle, surely, should be that all Canadians have a right to bid on contracts for the supply of goods and services to the public.
The hon. member who spoke last referred to hypocrisy in amended terms. Since the minister has failed to agree with me that he has found the information which I suggested to him would be found on his files, I want to read a letter I wrote on January 29, 1959. I do not know Mr. Pageau personally,

but he is one of the officials of the department with whom I had a good deal of correspondence during the six years before the government changed. Mr. Pageau will tell the minister of the true circumstances which have existed in the Yukon since I have been representing that region. When I have been advised by Mr. Pageau that a certain contract was expiring, and asking for my recommendations, I have in every instance, with the one exception I mentioned, written to him and asked him to send the contract out for public tender call. I said in writing to one of my local executives on January 29, 1959- and it was on or about that date that 1 wrote to Mr. Pageau to the same effect-
The Yukon Progressive Conservative association supports the proposition that when these mail contracts come up for renewal, they should go out to public tender so that all who are interested may have an equal opportunity to bid on them. As you know, this was not always so in the past and there are still some mail contracts in Yukon which have been automatically renewed, thus precluding the opportunity which all citizens in the Yukon have a right to expect, viz., the opportunity to bid on all public works on an equal basis. We have always stood for this principle which, I think you will agree, is a fair one.
This is the stand which I took and which I have taken since I was elected to represent the Yukon, and I think the minister would be well advised to revert to that practice. If he does not care to do so nationally, or if he has trouble with his own backbenchers over this aspect of patronage, then at least let him do me the courtesy of treating the people of the Yukon in an equal and fair fashion.
In addition, I should like to ask the minister a further question. I learned from this correspondence which has been tabled that the postmistress in Carmacks has been dismissed. I should like to know why. In the letter advising Mr. Wylie of the dismissal, the acting director of personnel states:
This is to inform you that instructions are being issued for a transfer of the Carmacks, Yukon, post office to Mrs. B. McKay as postmaster provided she possesses the necessary qualifications and can meet the requirements of the department.
I want to know if one of those qualifications is that she must be a Liberal.
Political fitness.

Perhaps that is one of the qualifications. Most likely it is; I do not know. The people of Carmacks were getting good service. I dare say that if a petition were circulated, like the one which the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac had sent to him, it would be found that the people of Carmacks were satisfied with the service they were getting. I should like to know why this lady was dismissed, and I should like to know

whether one of the qualifications of Mrs. McKay is that she is politically acceptable to the Postmaster General.
I have a further point to bring to the minister's attention. The wages that are paid to seasonal post office workers in the southern parts of Canada amount to 85 cents an hour. The wages paid to permanent personnel in the north are, of course, subject to supplementation by isolated post allowances; but these allowances do not apply to the seasonal staff earning 85 cents an hour. The same rate applies in the north. It was the hon. member for the Northwest Territories, who is also concerned about this, who drew the matter to my attention. If he speaks he may have something to say about it as well.
So I should like the minister to look into the question of those contracts. First, the Ross River contract. Why was that not put out to public tender, thus giving all Canadians an equal chance to bid in connection with this public service. The second was the contract for the carriage of mail between Dawson Creek and Whitehorse. The third was the contract for the carriage of mail between Whitehorse and Alaska Highway. That one, I assume, has already been awarded because it was on September 30, 1963, that it expired. I think I should also like to ask the minister to agree with my statement that in every case where contracts were called for public tender in the Yukon in the last six years there has been an actual saving in the taxpayers money by so doing.
I want to say a word or two about a matter referred to by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce. Patronage is a wrong principle on which to operate. I do not care whether it originated in 1867 or whether it was carried on throughout the whole of the years since that date. It should be dispensed with and disposed of by every government department, and there should be equal opportunity for all Canadians. I can remember a phrase which sticks in my mind, one of those phrases responsible for my getting into politics six or seven years ago. It was: "Fairness to all and favours to none". That is a sound principle and one which should be followed in all government activities. The minister's biggest single shortcoming in connection with this whole business of the production of lists and the question of patronage was the fact that he told the house when the matter was first referred to that there were no such lists. Then, on subsequent occasions, he admitted the existence of the list. Finally, belatedly, he produced the list. I feel that the minister has misled the members of the house, as the hon. member for Grey-Bruce put it. I think he should have resigned when it was suggested to him.
Supply-Post Office
Certainly, not only the Prime Minister but all the occupants of the treasury benches are implicated. Surely it is not proper conduct for any member occupying the treasury benches to say that something does not exist which actually does exist. Not only did he deny the existence of the list, but when he finally admitted its existence he actually tabled it. This sort of conduct falls a good deal short of what I feel Canadians expect of a minister. Certainly, the tenure of the Postmaster General must be short indeed. I think his days are numbered. I feel the Prime Minister should have taken some action at the time when it became apparent the minister had misled the house. I certainly do not expect to see the Postmaster General after Christmas. I do say that, brief as the minister's stay in the department might have been, he cannot in all conscience expect to remain there after Christmas. I should like, therefore, to wish the minister bon voyage and Merry Christmas.

Mr. Chairman, it is with the utmost sincerity that, first, I wish to congratulate the minister for having been appointed to the high post he now occupies.
I have many personal reasons to offer him my congratulations. To begin with, he was born in my constituency, where the Denis family is highly thought of, in addition to being held in great respect by your humble servant.
I have no intention of delaying the adoption of the Post Office estimates, but, very briefly, I should like to bring up three points about which I would appreciate his opinion or that of the officials of his department. Here, incidentally, I want to congratulate those people for the excellent job they are doing and the efforts they are making to continually improve the postal service throughout the country.
First of all, I would like to tell the Postmaster General about the numerous protests we received, in particular from citizens in the province of Quebec, against the possible removal of the words "postes" and "postage" from the stamps. I believe that many members received such protests from all corners of the province.
In my opinion, there is an advantage to keeping this visible proof of bilingualism in Canada. I wonder if the hon. minister could review that decision, whether it was taken by him or by officials in his department. I am sure also that his colleagues in the Liberal party made representations to him in that respect. It is to be hoped that no change will be made in the printing of the stamps and

Supply-Post Office
that those inscriptions will remain as they are now.
I should also like to ask the minister whether it would not be possible to suggest to the officials of his department to take into consideration, when assessing the value of mail contracts, not only the route but also the volume of mail to be delivered.
For a few years now, the Postmaster General has always considered distance as a primary factor in the case of a letter carrier but I think that today, in view of the ever-increasing volume of circulars and printed matter of all sorts which has to be delivered by the carrier, the officials of the department should also take into consideration the time it takes him to deliver his mail.
The Post Office Department should also consider a reclassification of post offices, especially semi-staff offices, where revenue is less than $3,000. I submit that the department should take into consideration the continuous increase in the cost of living, municipal taxes, rents, heating and electricity, so that in estimating the salary to be paid a postmaster whose revenue is less than $3,000, allowance be made also of the cost of living and of the various items I have just mentioned. Moreover, allowance should be made of the work that the postmaster is required to do in order to give satisfaction to the people he must serve as a postmaster.
Those are, Mr. Chairman, the few remarks I intended to address to the minister. And since there are reports that this house might be deprived of the presence of the minister in the relatively near future, I hope that if he is going to leave us, he will at least go to a more quiet place than this house. If that should happen, one cannot but bid him goodbye and wish him every success.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments to discuss a problem which, I think, is of interest to the house.
There are reports-and some people told me that it was a fact-that it was decided in the Social Credit party that every member of the house should give to the party coffers an amount of $3,000 taken out of their salaries. We have no objection to that at all. But I have heard that among them some had objected. I wonder if it is not the reason why some members of that party take liberties which, I think, are disgraceful, as far as the postal service is concerned.
I wish to refer more precisely to the fact that certain members take the liberty of using their franking privileges to distribute to Canadian taxpayers in certain constituencies their political propaganda. In this particular instance, it is about a publication of 50 pages or so, like this one, entitled

"Proposition de reformes monetaires, Credit social", which has been mailed by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Belanger).
I do not see any objection to the Social Credit trying to save its sinking boat. However, Mr. Chairman, I should not like the Canadian taxpayer to pay for that propaganda.
May I quote the note which Mr. Antoine Belanger, member of parliament for Charlevoix, has forwarded to hundreds of residents of the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay together with a copy of a publication like this one.
After receiving one of those booklets a voter in the riding of Charlevoix asked me to protest in the house, if you please, and to tell the member for Charlevoix that if he insisted on annoying people with such propaganda, the least he could do would be to stop making them pay for this mail service.
Mr. Chairman, this session is already well advanced, otherwise, I feel that the hon. member should be called before the committee on privileges and elections of this house. However, since it is getting late, I hope he will note these protests and immediately stop using public funds and the postage-free mailing service for such doubtful political proga-ganda as that of the Social Credit party.
I see that my hon. friends opposite seem to have fun because I accuse the members of the Social Credit party. Well, hon. members opposite should indeed feel that the hat fits them also, because they have also been guilty of this unfairness to the taxpayers.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I should ask the hon. member for Three Rivers to alter part of his last statement, and that is to replace the name "Social Credit" by the expression "Ralliement Creditistes."
It is with great pleasure that I accept that suggestion.
Mr. Chairman, I also rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member for Three Rivers just quoted a Social Credit pamphlet distributed by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Belanger).
At the expense of the state.

I bring to the attention of the house the fact there is a difference between doctrine publicity mailed by the hon. member for Charlevoix and the purely political propaganda distributed at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers by the Conservatives when they were in power.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. members will agree that there is no question of privilege here and I ask the hon. member for Three Rivers to continue.

If it was done in the past, that is no excuse to do it now.
The hon. member for Villeneuve proved nothing and only made a wild charge. I have here a letter from the hon. member for Charlevoix. I think it is scandalous to use Canadian public funds for such propaganda.
As for our hon. friends opposite, I should simply like to call their attention to those intriguing letters sent all over the province. It is an insult for the Canadian people when the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Cadieux) speaks about a great member of parliament, the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau), chairman of the caucus, and reports on all his activities. Reference is also made to the Prime Minister and the newspapers of this country are asked to use that propaganda paper to heave this country out of the mess it is in.
Indeed, the time has come to put a stop to such practices. Let us think of the taxpayer and do away with such practices.

Mr. Chairman, through you I would like to say to the minister that a few years ago I enjoyed very much participating with him in another activity when he was the captain of a bowling team of which I was a member. He is a good bowler; in fact he is a better bowler than he is a Postmaster General, if his first few months in office are any indication.
I am improving every day.

The minister says he is improving every day. If he improves every day as a bowler that is not possible, because in the first place he is a prime bowler; but if he says he is improving every day as a Postmaster General, all I say is that he cannot do anything else but go up, when he is at the bottom. However, I do hope that the remarks about his departure are not well founded and that he stays with the government, with his present post, so that in time to come we can see whether or not he and his government do improve.
Unfortunately, the hon. member for Hamilton East does not appear to be in the chamber, but I would like to make a few comments about his remarks. Initially let me say I agree with them, in so far as conduct of this kind is concerned. It makes me wonder, though, whether the hon. member for Hamilton East, and others of his party, would have the same views if the Conservatives had not had the discretion to disclose the patronage or consultant list in the first place. But once it has been disclosed, I think he tried to make the best of an awkward situation.
I do not want to deal with that list in any way at all, except to attempt to be helpful
Supply-Post Office
to the Postmaster General. I would say to him that if he is going to maintain such a list of consultants, and if he wants to use that list for greater efficiency in the operation of his department, I would be very happy if he would consult with me about the person on that list from Skeena, because I can name many more competent people than the one he has presently listed.
The person on the list is neither able, competent nor interested in assisting any of the activities of the office of the Postmaster General and, apart from that, he does not live in the riding, but rather in Duncan on Vancouver island, and has relatively little contact with the constituency. Now, he might make a good consultant for my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, if he so desires, but I would be happy to talk privately with the minister, or express publicly now, alternate consultants for Skeena if the minister wishes me to help him.
I should like to confine the remainder of my remarks to one phase of the activities of the department which was very disturbing to many members of parliament when it was first instituted. I am referring to the so-called spy system in some of the post offices throughout the country, the system whereby closed circuit television cameras are used-if that is the mechanism that is used-and one-way mirrors or peepholes to permit officials of the department to spy upon the activities of other employees in the department in the functions that they carry out during their work day.
This of course is automatically an invasion of the right of an individual to privacy. It casts serious reflection and doubts upon the honesty of employees in the minister's department, and it is even more nefarious than that when these mechanisms for spying are installed in the washrooms in some post offices.
Male or female?
My hon. friend will have to ask the Postmaster General about that point.
How do you know they exist?

I know they exist because I take the word of members of the cabinet who have proclaimed in this house that they do exist, and the word of people in the Post Office Department to whom I have spoken and who say they exist. But the interjection by the hon. member opposite about whether these are placed in male or female washrooms, or both, does raise the question of what sort of people are employed to use these spying mechanisms, and what is the classification given by the civil service commission to individuals within the post office structure-

Supply-Post Office
who actually do the spying into washrooms in the department, spying on the activities of the individuals who use the washroom facilities. There are some who have particular aptitudes which one might class as voyeuristic, and who might fit well into this category. But whether or not people with perverted ideas about what should take place in washrooms are employed in using these spying mechanisms, it should be disclosed. I understand from the communications that have been sent to me, and from discussions I have had with employees, that they are concerned about two things. They are concerned (1), about the system of spying upon them, because it is an invasion of their privacy, especially when it takes place in washrooms; and (2), they are concerned about the type of individual or just who it is who is watching them, as Big Brother is supposed to watch people, through peepholes or one-way mirrors to see what is taking place there. I think it is a regrettable situation that the Post Office Department has to engage in this sort of activity, which casts doubt upon the honesty of all the employees concerned and places them under a continual, daily cloud of suspicion even in so far as their most private moments are concerned.
I now wish to turn to another matter, Mr. Chairman. I have had a number of exchanges of correspondence with the minister about individual, local problems that exist in Skeena. I do not want to relate them all now to the minister or the committee, or place them on Hansard, so far as the pertinent details are concerned; but I do wish to make general reference to the fact that we have in the riding of Skeena communities which have a once a month postal service; once every month, in some of the communities, mail is delivered and once a month it is taken out again. This means that people often have to wait a month or a month and a half before they can deal adequately with any piece of correspondence. I am sure that people who are used to getting mail delivered on a daily basis would, if they just reflected on this and thought how it would be if their mail were delivered on a monthly basis, realize the inconvenience that exists for these people. In this enlightened day I think that to continue a system which has been in existence for many years now, namely mail delivery on a once a month basis to communities in this nation, is an unconscionable thing.
We have other communities in which the regularity of mail, as the minister knows, is twice a month, or on a two weeks basis. That is only half as bad as it is on the basis of *once a month. We have situations in which mail cannot be delivered directly from one point to another, but you can look across the water and see the community to which

you want a letter delivered. In spite of the proximity, you find it is impossible to put a letter in the mail and have it carried across perhaps two or three miles of water, even though a boat goes every day. You find it cannot be delivered to the other point directly, but instead it has to go 500 miles by air to Vancouver, wait in Vancouver overnight, be put on exactly the same plane that took it there the day before, and be brought the 500 miles back again to be delivered to a place that, as I say, you can look across two or three miles of water and see.
I think this is an unfair imposition upon people who happen to live in communities which are relatively more isolated than, say, large urban cities such as Montreal, Ottawa, or any of the other many, many communities and municipalities in Canada. I do not want to put all these things on the public record item by item or relate them orally to the minister now. We have had correspondence about them. The answer I received from the minister, though beautifully phrased and encompassing an entire page, winds up really saying that no change is going to be made to correct this situation. While I have communicated with the minister about this and intend to do so again, at this stage I wish only to ask him orally to please do something to correct this situation. If in this day and age people have to wait a month at a time to deal with their correspondence, it is a sad situation. They would like to see this matter straightened out, and I am sure the minister would also. If he would apply himself as assiduously to this question of providing adequate mail services to these relatively isolated and small communities as he applied himself to the job when he was captain of the bowling team of which I was a member, this problem would be solved before the end of the year.

Mr. Chairman, I was happy to hear the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro) state a while ago that the names of members from third parties do not appear on the patronage lists. In fact, I noticed that we are not on the list of the chairman of committees nor on that of the deputy chairman of committees either because we had to wait until a number of members had concluded their remarks before we could have the floor ourselves. Anyhow, we do not complain about that because our conscience is clear since we are not included in any list.
Mr. Chairman, I think the Postmaster General's (Mr. Denis) ordeal is practically over. I shall be brief since, unlike the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), we did not have the privilege of securing official

correspondence. We believe there has been a leak somewhere, but we do not know where.
It was simply given by the government.
Mr. Chairman, I am told that it was simply given by the government. I am well pleased-
All you had to do was to ask for it, by putting a notice of motion on the order paper.

Mr. Chairman, when I
phoned my wife last night, I learned that someone who had asked for a letter of introduction during the weekend wished to have another letter. I must say that this letter was not to be sent to the Post Office Department, but rather to the Department of Transport-at least, I believe that it was to be sent to the Department of Transport; any way, it was not for the Post Office Department.
Finally, it appears that when the individual in question came to apply for a job, another letter was asked of him because the one he had was not good. They suggested he obtain a letter from the Liberal member in the constituency. Then, for the first time, I learned it was possible to have two kinds of members in my constituency: the member who was elected under the Social Credit tag, and another one who was supposed to have been elected under the Liberal tag.
And they even insisted to give his name. When it was mentioned it was lawyer Ovide Laflamme, my wife understood immediately it was not the Liberal member for the constituency, but the defeated Liberal candidate. I hope this elector was lucky enough to obtain a letter from the defeated candidate, since he was really in need. As far as I am concerned, I thought I could have helped in recommending him. I hope my hon. opponent agreed to give him a letter, so that he could obtain the job in question, since the recommendation from the member does not seem sufficient.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to insist too much on the question of patronage, since it is currently discussed, and is a state of affairs of which everybody is aware. We are still in the era of the "believe or die", when qualifications are more often based on political allegiance or existing lists than ability to fill the job.
I think it is time to put a stop to such a procedure, especially as members on both sides of the house spoke against that state of affairs, and I see no reason why the government should not decide, once and for all, to do away with those lists, or at least place them
Supply-Post Office
in secure places, so that the matter is not constantly heard of in the House of Commons.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal briefly with a problem concerning the Postmaster General.
A while ago, mention was made of new control or spying devices being used in the Post Office Department. I realize that such devices make it possible to spy, so to speak, into the private lives of many workers. However this does not necessarily mean that everybody is suspected. It simply means that all civil servants know there is a threat, a kind of sword of Damocles hanging over their heads, and that is for the purpose of preventing certain practices in use in the past. Maybe, it is a good thing, for fear is the beginning of wisdom. However, I hope that the department officials will never have to use those devices, since the employees know that they exist.
Mr. Chairman, I wish also to comment about the employees' efficiency rating. Naturally, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) did not talk about that since it is the policy of a socialist government to have efficiency and efficiency rating. But I would say that efficiency rating is more often contrary to personal freedom than the means of protection which we now have, just as our buildings are equipped with protection devices against fire or against theft.
It is a question of protecting the employees who, being human, are liable to make mistakes or be guilty of some indiscretion.
In any event, the use of some efficiency norms interfere with personal freedom because the employees concerned are labelled beforehand by the officials in the department.
In fact, certain civil servants think that such part of the work must be done in so-many minutes, that the employee should classify so many letters in a minute, in a quarter of an hour, or in an hour, and, in order to know whether that employee does his job well, inspectors are placed not behind spying machines, but in galleries next to the employee's place of work. I say this is. really a derogation to human freedom, and I believe people who work efficiently should be trusted, especially when they work in an atmosphere where they have the feeling they are useful to the government and the public. I believe those people are able to do their work without always having inspectors watching them for efficiency.
I also wish to quote the case of certain extra workers hired for the Christmas season, for instance, sometimes through their member and sometimes through the defeated candidate, sometimes directly through the postmaster, which evidently may give rise to criticism. However, I wish to point out

Supply-Post Office that some voters in my constituency, who applied to their member were refused employment, while others were accepted because their letters of recommendation came from somewhere else.
There are also additional employees. In my constituency, I have heard of people having worked on a part time basis and rendered great services and then being told, after a year, that they had to be replaced since their job was only temporary. And they were replaced by other workers at a lower salary, as the latter had no claim to the increase which had been granted to their predecessors. As I said, I do not think it is a matter of a man's efficiency but rather a matter of discrimination for various reasons unknown to me.
Before closing, I should like to remind the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen)- whom as I have learned recently has been nicknamed Yukon Eric-that the whole Post Office Act should be completely amended and not the minister's attitude, because the act authorizes the minister to renew contracts without calling tenders, provided he is satisfied with the performance under existing contracts. That, of course, is left to his discretion. If he does not want to renew a contract, he can call tenders.
I made a thorough study of the Post Office Act last year because several cases were referred to me where people had lost their contract following a call for tenders while others could not get a contract even when they made a bid because the previous *contract had been automatically renewed. I think it would be appropriate for parliament to take a look at the Post Office Act in order to put an end to that situation.
Before I resume my seat, I should like to wish good luck to the minister. No matter where he goes in the next few years, I am positive everybody would want to wish him well.

Mr. Chairman, I also would have been very pleased to congratulate the Postmaster General. However, the few comments I intend to make would not justify such congratulations, and that is why I shall refrain from offering any.
I have no intention either of speaking about patronage-the word patronage seems to grate -on the ear of the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro). I feel I have to speak of arrogance. One may be taxed with arrogance if, when duty-bound to inform somebody, he refrains from doing so by dodging the issue or hiding behind the rules.
At the beginning of October, in a speech I had described the Postmaster General as a

real champion of patronage within the Liberal party, and I think that title fits him like a glove.
Earlier, the hon. member for the Yukon indicated that when the matter of a list of consultants in the Post Office Department came up in the house, the minister answered that there was no patronage list but he admitted a week later that there was such a list of consultants. It was even suggested, in some quarters, following that change of mind, that this would almost call for a resignation and that, in all fairness, the Postmaster General should resign. Some newspapers even dared to ask for such a resignation.
I should like to tell the house that that was not the only time the Postmaster General was not accurate in his answers.
As reported on page 676 of Hansard I asked the Postmaster General the following question:

2.	Were the changes that have been carried out provided for in the plan originally accepted?
3.	Are the changes to the initial project expected to increase the cost?
4.	What is the estimated cost of the increased expenditures brought about by these changes?
5.	Why was the original project changed after it had been accepted?
Here is the answer given by the deputy postmaster general:
1.	Part of the structure had to be rebuilt due to an error in the plans.
2.	No.
3.	Yes.
4.	$2,450.
5.	Because, in the original plans, the floor level was too low as compared with the sidewalk level.
As reported on page 3743 of Hansard for October 18, 1963, I asked an oral question, following those answers. Here it is:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct my question to the Postmaster General, to whom I have given notice.
My question relates to the one bearing number G20, which appeared on the order paper and which has been answered.
What person or persons have been consulted for the choice of the architect responsible for the building of the Beauceville post office in the county of Beauce?
And here is the answer:
That is a question for the order paper-

Again I put on the order paper a series of questions which can be found at page 4669 of Hansard for November 13, 1963. Mr. Chairman, I wish to point out here that those questions were identical, in form as well as contents, to those asked by all the other members of the Ralliement Creditistes. All other members who had put similar questions got the appropriate answers with figures.
Here is question No. 1,428:
1.	How many contracts have been let, or for how many contracts have bids been called by the Post Office Department since April 8, 1963, tor the constituency of Beauce?
2.	Who were the bidders on these contracts?
3.	What were the bids of each of them?
4.	To whom were the contracts let?
5.	Who was responsible for distribution of tender forms?
The answers were as follows:
1. None. 2. Not applicable. 3. Not applicable. 4. Not applicable. 5. Not applicable.
I am the only one to have obtained such an answer. However, following the production of the list of consultants, I put another question asking for the tabling of documents. I have here the whole list of correspondence, as well as contracts reviewed from April 30, 1963 until November 1963.
I have here a written contract dated September 18, 1963, and sent to Mr. Jean-Paul Racine, in St. Honore de Shenley. I quote: Dear Mr. Racine,
A request for an increase in salary has been submitted by Mr. Joseph Gagnon, mail transportation contractor operating between St. Georges West and Vallee Junction.
The case having been carefully reviewed, it is felt that $1,800 would be a just retribution for the work done. That would represent an annual increase of $251.
Consequently, the department intends to bring up Mr. Gagnon's salary from $1,549 to $1,800 a year, as from September 1, 1963.
The list continues, and it is rather a long one. It is addressed to the former Liberal candidate in Beauce county, who gives us an official answer. Now, as recorded in Hansard of November 13, 1962, the minister says exactly the opposite, that is that there was no exchange of letters, no contracts let.
That is why I say that that he is hiding behind standing orders to avoid answering questions which are entitled to a clear, precise and exact answer; I feel that in the present instance, the minister does not deserve from me any of the congratulations which other hon. members have lavished upon him.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to make, and I was anxious to make them because I am the only one to have received such an answer to questions similar to those asked by other hon. members.
