If this is not a sort of patronage, then I think the word "arrogance" would be the most appropriate word for such a way of doing things on the part of the Postmaster General.
I heard the hon. member for Villeneuve say that the minister was, in the good old days, in 1946, a member of the Little Chicago in the house.
Well, in my opinion, the title I gave him in a speech I made in the house, in October, suited him perfectly.
I do not want to speak of patronage, but I can say that it is after many such arrogant actions that we, Social Crediters, have the right to say that if the people were aware of everything that goes on in the lobbies, they would not put up any longer with the old line parties in the house.
I was listening a while ago to the remarks of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) who said that, in a newspaper report, mention was made of $3,000 for our election coffers. In reply to this assertion, I can say that the old line parties also have coffers supplied from sources whose origin we sometimes know. That is why I do not hesitate to answer back that even though it were true that some members of the Ralliement Creditistes contribute to the activities of their movement in the province of Quebec, this is no reason to make charges; far from it, this is all to their credit.
Besides, certain political parties get their funds in Canada and even, sometimes, out of the country.
However, if these gentlemen think that it is in order to heave off our boat, I hope that it will not be the Three Rivers ferry that will change the situation, but the bridge that will be built with the shortest possible delay.
You will appreciate that with such arrogance, it is impossible for me to congratulate him about the way the officials responsible for the lists of consultants act. Here, I agree with the hon. member for Villeneuve when he says that it would be normal, when letters are exchanged in a riding which have to do with the spending of public funds, that the member for the riding be at least informed through a copy of the letter, even if they want to send one to the consultant, in order that he may know what goes on.
Those are the remarks I wanted to make. Whatever the result of the approval of the Postmaster General's estimates, I nevertheless wish him the greatest possible success should he be called to take on other duties, which would be a normal reward after some 30 years in politics. He deserves our whole sympathy, even if sometimes he does not get

Supply-Post Office
our congratulations tor a certain kind of work. I wish him, as did others, to enjoy at last the quietness he deserves.

Mr. Chairman, it is always interesting to speak on any departmental estimates, especially the estimates of the Post Office Department, for the simple reason that before being elected to the House of Commons as representative of Waterloo North I was postmaster and supervisor at Elmira for nearly 36 years. During that time I saw a great many changes. I understand that there are over 50,000 people employed in 12,000 post offices, and the postage required to handle the mail brings in revenues of more than half a million dollars each day. The greatest asset of the department is its nation-wide family of postal workers, and the principal reason for the respect with which the department is regarded by the people of Canada is the devoted service which this great body of men and women has given. Such service has played an important part in the nation's development. It has provided the all-important communications system without which our country could not have achieved its present growth and prosperity. We know that the Post Office Department can never be static, but I am sure that the future will see many more changes, and constructive changes at that. These changes rest not only upon new machinery and equipment but upon the traditional spirit of devotion to duty which has always characterized our postal employees, and the personal sense of responsibility on the part of each member of the service.
I was very much disturbed by the report that patronage is creeping into the service more than ever. I might say that if this is the case it could be the most damnable disaster which could ever happen to the Post Office Department. It has been brought to my attention that the federal association of letter carriers is protesting the disciplinary policy of the Post Office Department and, in particular, the sentencing of employees to salary reductions for petty or unintentional discrepancies. I understand that "unknown checks" are to be carried out on letter carriers-in other words, spying-and that salary reductions will be recommended for the least error. Surely such tactics are altogether unwarranted and I hope the department will abolish this type of punishment.
I am sure we all agree that people making applications for positions should have all the qualifications necessary for the work required and that these appointments should be approved by the civil service commission without interference from anyone. This is the only

way in which this great service will be able to continue for the benefit of all people in Canada.
Most of us think of our postal service merely as an organization for transmitting mail, and though we may have daily contact with postal employees very few of us realize how extensive are its services and how diversified are its functions.
The size and scope of Canada's post office can be indicated by the following example. Let hon. members imagine, if they can, the combined weight of a thousand diesel locomotives. This would amount to slightly less than the weight of mail handled daily. As I have previously mentioned, there are over 12,000 post offices across the country. In some of our major cities these offices employ upwards of 4,500 people. In many other centres they are located in a general store or other central place where the only postal employee is a part-time postmaster.
More than any other government department or agency the Post Office Department is in direct daily contact with almost every Canadian, delivering each year an average of 225 letters for almost every Canadian man, woman and child in this country.
The previous government saw the need of improvements to the postal service in my constituency of Waterloo North, as well as in other places. We have a new post office in Kitchener, now nearing completion. We have one in Waterloo and, I understand, plans are being made for one in Elmira.
Perhaps one of the most important changes in postal rates was the four-cent local or drop letter rate of postage between Kitchener and Waterloo which was approved by the former postmaster general. In my remarks of April 13, 1961, which will be found in Hansard on page 3653, I referred to the possible application of the minimum four-cent local or drop letter postage between these twin cities. As members can understand, Kitchener and Waterloo at that time were classed as two separate and distinct postal areas. This has been of great importance to these twin cities, as well as others across Canada, and also has meant a great deal to the larger firms. Suboffices are a great asset to any city, and Kitchener has had some new ones which have provided excellent service to people in such localities. Waterloo had its first such office installed under the previous government, and another one added some time later. I feel that Waterloo with its 22,000 people should have more than two such offices.
I would like to congratulate the Postmaster General on his appointment and, as a former employee, let me say I well understand that his position could become the most important in the government. Over the past five years,

while sitting in opposition, he asked the former postmaster general many questions during orders of the day. Yes, and some of them were of very little interest or value. I trust, now, that he will be ready, and indeed anxious, to answer any questions which may be put to him in his turn. I understand that the degree of activity since April 8 within this department has been, generally, nominal. In fact, a list of the activities which have been undertaken would include only a couple of new stamp issues, an extension of the stamp issue program and an increase in the posted rates governing a variety of items. The increase in registration fees is, no doubt, in keeping with the times, as is the increase in special delivery fees. However, I feel the increase is too severe. It could cost some of the larger firms thousands of dollars. The working man, with his small income, could also object to such a jump, as could the small businessman.
The rates of postage on third class mail and the fees on C.O.D. are to be increased as of April 1, 1964. I believe these changes should have been made effective on the same date as the changes affecting registration and special delivery, in which case the government might have increased its revenue by about $10 million during the Christmas season.
For some time I have been asking that parttime assistance in the post office could be employed through the civil service commission in the same way as full time employees. If this were done, these workers would probably give better service and they would also have the opportunity of enjoying superannuation benefits after they retire. At present, this is not possible. A number of years ago I had a lady working with me in my office. She was a part time employee. This lady is still employed there, and on her retirement she will walk out without superannuation or any benefits whatever. Surely such people should be given some compensation on leaving their positions.
I was interested to learn about the new promotion opportunities for postal employees as announced by the Postmaster General. In future, vacancies at semi-staff group 33 offices, of which there are 210 in Canada, will be filled by competition open to postal employees in the postal district. In the past, these positions have been open only to the residents of the community where the vacancy occurred. This is a welcome move. However, I believe this should also apply to members of the groups 30, 31, and 32 whose work is similar to that of the 33 group.
Another suggestion I should like to make is this, that the competition be extended to the whole province and not only to the district
Supply-Post Office
concerned. This will give a greater opportunity to postmasters and assistants in the lower group of semi-staff post offices who have the qualifications to compete for such positions. The present move will be welcomed by the Canadian postmasters association of which I was a member for many years. The officers and executives of this association have for a long time dedicated their services to the welfare of all employees, and former postmasters general under the previous government have recognized the valuable work of this association for the betterment of the postal service. I hope the present minister will accept the co-operation of this body and give careful consideration to all the suggestions which it brings forward.
The former government played a great part in making possible the progress of this department. In 1961-62, the volume of mail handled remained high. More than 4 billion pieces were processed. Revenue in that year amounted to $213,579,446 and represented an increase of $11,575,655 over the previous year. A revision in parcel post rates accounted for $8,600,000 and additional mailings of U.S. publications in Canada accounted for $1,400,000. The farsightedness of the previous government is best exemplified by the construction of the Sir Alexander Campbell building which brought the various divisions under one roof and allowed, for the first time, for a more closely knit organization with better interoffice communication and co-ordinated working facilities. The postage meter system was increased, or extended, in 1961-62 to an additional 62 offices. My former office in Elmira joined in such progress, which gives many firms the opportunity of using this service. I understand that this mechanical method of pre-paying postage is now installed in 1,163 Canadian post offices.
In the fiscal year, 1961-62, construction of 110 small and large post office buildings was completed, while 52 were under construction at the end of the year. The number of post offices accommodated in federal buildings as of March, 1962 was 1,121, while 940 offices were accommodated in leased quarters.
An important part of the progress made in 1961-62 concerned the letter carrier walks whose number was increased by 230. It now totals 104,603. The total number of calls has increased by 104,603 and totalled 2,999,969 at the end of 1961-62.
As a postmaster for over 35 years, and also supervisor of smaller offices in my district, I well recognize the fine work being done by all such supervisors. Such work was carried out by the former area superintendents, but there has been a change and now such work, as I mentioned, is being carried out by these postmasters.

Supply-Post Office
The employees and the department have played a great part in the constant advancement and progress of this fine Post Office Department. Few of us realize how extensive are its services and how diversified are its functions. It has expanded, changed and adapted itself to the physical and economic growth of the nation. I may say to the Postmaster General that I hope in his travels he will visit all the smaller offices, as the former postmaster general did, and in that way become acquainted with the members of the staff and the work that should be done. From the smallest of beginnings, the Post Office Department has grown to a complex nationwide organization that penetrates into the most remote corners of the country, swiftly and efficiently knitting together the threads of our national fabric. Yes, Canada's post office has an extremely appropriate motto: Service to the public.
In order that this advancement may continue, may I point out to the Postmaster General that all appointments must be made by the civil service commission, so that all applying for such work may have an equal chance of success according to their qualifications.

Mr. Chairman, in taking part in this debate, I can assure you that it is not my intention to delay the proceedings of the house very long.
First of all, I would like to take this opportunity to greet the hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Choquette), who occasionally visits us in this house. I would like to ask him to be indulgent and to listen to my few remarks.
I would also take this opportunity to congratulate the Postmaster General (Mr. Denis) for the confidence put on him by his leader when he entrusted him with the administration of one of the most important departments of the government, that of the post office. I was glad of that promotion which has been given him.
I have been one of the first to know him, and it was then both of us were delegates to the United Nations. I profited by his wide experience and his parliamentary life as well as by his sound advice and his company, for he is a very merry man, whom it is always a pleasure to meet. I believe that newspaperman Mr. Marcel Gingras, of "La Presse", has given proper credit to that personality in one of his recent life stories.
I would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute and at the same time thank the officials of the Post Office Department who are always at our disposal to help us with all the problems which we submit to them.

I can only say that my relations with them, and with the department as well, have always been most friendly, for we always succeeded together to solve the few problems which we had to discuss.
However, I wish that the Postmaster General had not, in his everyday work, preferred to follow the suggestions coming from outside rather than those formulated by the elected members of the house who deal with public affairs.
I feel that the minister would do well to change his attitude and to pass through elected representatives instead. As far as I am concerned, I can assure him that I would not abuse the privilege since I have only one ambition here, that is to serve my electors as well as I can.
Mr. Chairman, I wholeheartedly agree with what the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) said. I shall not repeat the suggestions and recommendations he made to the minister but I should like to take this opportunity to stress certain inaccuracies and contradictions made by the minister in some of his statements concerning the increase in postal rates.
If my memory serves me well, he laid the blame on the wrong party at the time. He may not have used those very words but he nevertheless tried to convince his audience that the increase was due to lack of administrative ability by his predecessor at the head of the Post Office Department.
Like the hon. member who spoke before me, I regret the increases which the minister recommended because they are costly for the public. In the long run, Canadian taxpayers will have to foot the bill.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to remind the minister that when he was sitting on this side of the house, he did not miss a chance to advocate mail delivery twice a day. I wish to point out that it is now within his power to restore that service.
I congratulate the minister for having obtained salary increases for certain classes of employees, but I should like to associate myself with those who deplore the fact that he has not used his influence a little more, since this pay boost of $60 gives the parties concerned only 17 cents more per day. Everyone will agree that is not much, and the good job done by those people should have been better rewarded. As I say, the minister should have brought more pressure to bear and obtained a larger increase for his employees.
Mr. Chairman, since the Christmas season is almost here, I would ask the minister to kindly help me give a practical gift to the residents of four important parishes of my riding.

I refer to the parishes of St. Denis, St. Damase, St. Rosalie and Upton. With the co-operation of the minister, we could give those parishes a building for the post office, which the citizens of those parishes would welcome.
Mr. Chairman, in closing my remarks, I will say that, should the rumours whispered around parliament hill materialize, I join with other members of parliament to wish a most agreeable and most pleasant journey to my friend, the hon. member for St. Denis, Postmaster General.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks are going to be as brief as possible, as I know the Postmaster General desires to have his estimates passed before this day's sitting finishes. I take this opportunity of congratulating him on the presentation of his first estimates. For a number of years I have enjoyed a friendly association with him in an organization that has previously been mentioned, the House of Commons bowling league, and I feel possibly I may have brought him along up to the presidency of that league because he followed me in that office. Our associations in it were very pleasant and I hope they will continue to be that way.
Before going further I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Waterloo North, who this afternoon presented what I think was the second report on the Post Office Department, outlining in a very excellent way the activities of the department as carried out in previous years, and this was but rightly so because he is the only member of the House of Commons who was a P.M.- a postmaster-before he became an M.P.
The hon. member for Danforth brought a matter to the attention of the committee that I also wish to speak about, the reasons letter carriers are at the present time asking for a salary increase, collective bargaining and compulsory arbitration.
I do not know whether the hon. member brought to the attention of the committee that these requests were contained in a letter put forth by branch No. 1 of the Toronto association, but I do wish to support his remarks for the reason that branch 23 of the federated association of letter carriers of St. Thomas has also endorsed this letter and asked for the same consideration.
I now want to turn to a few items of a local nature in my own constituency. Before doing so I cannot let the opportunity pass without mentioning something about patronage. I am not going to be critical of the minister, because I do not recall that any patronage has been practised in my riding since I
Supply-Post Office
became a member of parliament. But I suggest to the minister that he throw away that Liberal list of consultants and make a new list, which would have on it the elected members of parliament; because they are the men and women elected to represent their constituencies here and, if anyone is to be consulted, they are the ones who should be consulted about matters pertaining to their constituencies.
Patronage was not practised in the constituency of Elgin during the previous administration, and more especially it has not been practised in the matter of rural mail carrier contracts. There are over 40 rural mail contracts in the riding of Elgin and during the past 10 years since I was first elected, to the best of my knowledge only a few of those contracts came up for tender. The reason a tender is called is usually due to the death of a contractor. These men and women are doing an excellent job and they see that the mail is carried and delivered every day regardless of weather conditions; and we all know that weather conditions, especially at this time of the year, are not always the best.
When these rural contracts do come up every four years and a contractor is doing efficient work, then I feel consideration should be given to the renewal of his contract. Many contractors fail to ask for their contracts to be reviewed after they have been in force for two years. They are hesitant to do so because if they ask for a review and an increase in their contracts, they fear they will lose them at the end of four years, and if patronage is being practised they are hesitant to ask for the consideration which is rightly theirs.
I now wish to refer to an election promise made during the last two election campaigns by the Liberal candidate in my riding, that if a Liberal government were elected a new post office would be erected in the village of Vienna. Last June I put this question on the order paper and it was answered on June 12, question 350:
Is it the intention of the government to build a post office at Vienna, Ontario, this year?
The Postmaster General replied:
No. This is a revenue post office, group 24, where the postmaster is responsible for the provision of the premises as part of his remuneration.
That is probably quite correct but I feel that certain discrimination is being practised against the residents of this community because the present post office is contained in a room no longer than the table in front of me here, and I believe it is only eight feet wide. Three miles to the south, in the village of Port Burwell they have had a new post office for some time and, five miles on the other side, Staffordville, also

Supply-Post Office
has a new post office. Naturally the residents of Vienna cannot understand why these other two communities, one not nearly as large, have been able to obtain new post offices.
It is correct that under the present regulations the postmaster is supposed to provide the accommodation, but he has reached the age of retirement. He is now on extension and no doubt does not wish to go to great expense on his own behalf to provide accommodation that he may only occupy for a short period of time. I hope the minister will give serious consideration to see if some method can be worked out whereby this community can have a new post office.
The other item I wish to mention is the post office that has been promised for the village of West Lome. Over the past number of years the residents in West Lome have not been able to agree on a site, but in the neighbouring village of Rodney the Department of Public Works has already secured a site which has been cleared, and both town councils have agreed on it. I suggest that consideration be given to the building that was promised for West Lome, and I believe that in the estimates of the Department of Public Works provision is made for that. It would be of great benefit if it were built in Rodney where a site is already secured.

Mr. Chairman, at the beginning of these short remarks, I would like to congratulate the Postmaster General on his recent appointment. I hope that during his short term of office he will take steps to further the public interest and that of his department.
I would like to offer him a few suggestions and, if he takes them into account, he will be considered, in his brief tenure, as an excellent Postmaster General who works in the public interest, in his country's interest.
First, the Postmaster General could study the possibility of closing post offices on Saturday. That practice is followed by some financial establishments, including banks, in Canada. On the other hand, the government of the Netherlands decided recently to close post offices on Saturday.
Second, I ask him to find a way so that letter carriers will not have to climb stairs to deliver mail to people living on the second or third floors. In my opinion, an arrangement could be made with the landlords and the tenants to have mail boxes on the first floor, so that those postal employees would not have to work under such inhuman conditions. I realize that they have to serve the people but the Canadian people, I think, would appreciate any change which might make the letter carrier's work easier.
Third, the minister talked about new stamp designs. If he should like to have suggestions in that respect, he could ask the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette).
I would also ask the Postmaster General to find a way to prevent the Post Office Department from being used to distribute communist propaganda. This problem is not new. However, it should be possible to find a way to completely stop that communist propaganda which is distributed throughout the country. Canada spends millions of dollars on national defence, against our eastern enemies. Therefore I find it illogical to allow the Post Office Department to distribute communist propaganda.
Before coming to the end of my remarks, I would like to point out that some members on the government side use official House of Commons stationery, as well as envelopes, and the House of Commons frank to mail Liberal party propaganda. I have the evidence here:	House of Commons, Ottawa,
Canada. It is a letter mailed to weeklies in the province of Quebec and signed "Jean Berger, Montmagny-L'Islet, publicity agent of the Liberal party, Ottawa". And the amazing thing is that he used an envelope with the frank of the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Cadieux) on it.
I am of the opinion, Mr. Chairman, that government members should set the example and not have-

me. I did not know that the hon. member considered himself amongst the most uncompromising members. I take note of that. Now, coming back to the precise point he mentioned, I sent exact information to weekly newspapers, but I did not consider it necessary to mention the hon. member.
Order.

speechtext: Order. The hon. member will admit that this is not a question of privilege but an argument, and he will probably have the opportunity to submit it later.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks were quite polite. I quoted a document which truly exists and the hon. member had his secretary put underneath his signature-on paper paid for by the taxpayers-the typewritten inscription "Publicity agent of the Liberal party, Ottawa".
Mr. Chairman, before I resume my seat, I should like to quote an article which was published in the Ottawa Journal, on November 14, 1963, and which refers to a statement

made by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) who, as we all know, sits on the government side. The article, which deals with the abuses of the government and the patronage within the Post Office Department, reads as follows:

Dr. Jewett critical of politicians.
_ She said that the bids for rural postal routes, in particular, still operate under patronage.

Mr. Chairman, these were the few comments which I wanted to make and I hope that the Postmaster General will take up the suggestions which I made at the beginning. I would like to hear his comments.
Would the hon. member allow me to ask him a question?
Go on.
Has the hon. member ever sent a letter for propaganda or publicity purposes?

I did not make any publicity for my party in particular. I wrote to the local newspapers in Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, and this is my right and duty as a member to give to the people an account of the work done by your humble servant in the house, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take a few minutes of the time of the committee just to say that the Postmaster General has ignored every attempt to soften his heart and dispense with the old, Liberal party tradition of immediately firing everyone who dared to differ from their opinions or were even brave enough to express their own opinions. Many of these people, who are innocent of even being interested in politics, were dismissed because of the biased opinion of someone in their party or a member of their ranks. I could take up considerable time of the committee in telling hon. members of many such instances, but I will not because of experience in the past few weeks of complaints falling upon deaf ears. I also refrain from detailing these instances because I do not wish to take up the time of the committee. However, I take this opportunity, on behalf of the riding of Hastings-Frontenac, whose people are, I believe, the most loyal in the Dominion of Canada to our democratic way of life, to express to you, the Postmaster General, our good wishes for a very merry Christmas and a happy new year.

Mr. Chairman, I merely want to rise and make an appeal to the minister to consider the possibility of providing house to house deliveries in smaller ciites where the geographical circumstances warrant it.
28902-5-388
Supply-Post Office
I recognize that at the present time the regulations provide for only house to house deliveries in cities with a population of 5,000 and over. I believe that is the number. I have written to the present Postmaster General and to the previous postmaster general regarding the city of Port Moody, which is located along the Burrard inlet. Because there is a mountain on one side and the sea on the other, the city has had to stretch out over a considerable territory. The result is that many old people are 20 or 25 blocks away from the post office. I recognize that in many communities where there are 2,500 people in a compact area it is not much of a problem to go to the post office. But when a city because of its geographical features extends over a considerable territory this really works a hardship. I suggest to the minister that he take these geographical features into consideration. I do not think that the population figure alone ought to be the cut-off at which house to house delivery is provided. I should like to ask the minister to give some consideration to this point.
Carried.

May I say to the member who is saying "carried" that I have taken no part whatsoever in the discussion today and have taken none of the time of the committee. Therefore I reserve the right, if I choose to do so, to raise this matter with the Postmaster General at this time.

Item agreed to.
5. Operations including salaries and other expenses of staff post offices, district offices, railway mail service staffs, and supplies, equipment and other items for revenue post offices, including administration, $121,454,700.

Mr. Chairman, I am not sure whether the minister has referred to the matter of railway delivery but there is a great deal of dissatisfaction in my area with regard to the curtailment that is taking place in the sorting of mail on some railway runs. In my opinion this service has been a very satisfactory one. It was built up over a number of years and it has been particularly so in the case of small communities. Certainly this is true of places outside Toronto. I have had complaints of letters taking five days to be carried 100 miles. When letters to be carried from one community to another community ten or 15 miles away were sorted on railway mail cars the letters were put into a bag that was dropped off at the next point. If there are no sorting facilities the mail is sent to a terminal, is handled in that terminal and is returned, but only on trains providing the type of mail service involving delivery to each area.

Supply-Post Office
This has been a problem in northern Ontario. There is considerable discussion about removing one of the trips of one of the major trains out of Toronto at the present time. This will curtail most of the mail delivery that used to be made, by reason of the train running from Timmins to Toronto on Sunday. This will mean that in many cases it will take more than 24 hours for the mail to go to the terminal point, be sorted and returned.
Despite what Mr. Gordon and others may say, the railways are not operating on freight alone but also on express and mail carriage, and if they did not have the revenue from the branch lines serving the less populated areas they would not be able to show a profit of any kind. I think the Postmaster General has a great deal of influence with regard to the service that is being provided in this field.
It has been said that mail delivery has been speeded up by the use of road transportation. To my knowledge this has never been the case. It has not been advantageous for me to mail a letter from Ottawa to my riding by air. There would be no advantage in sending it by air because if the proper train connections can be made, delivery is much quicker. We think that a plea should be made for those engaged in the mail sorting service. If the service is discontinued we will in my opinion be catering to the large communities with central distribution offices and central sorting services without providing service to as many Canadians as possible, regardless of population and what facilities they themselves have.
You can put a letter on the train in Swastika, for instance, and if there is a sorting service on the train it will be delivered to the addressee in Englehart in the morning. If it is taken to North Bay it is not returned until the next morning. If there is still no drop-off service on the train it will go back to the centre it came from and be returned to the post office as bag mail. This could take 48 hours. You could walk the distance in several hours and carry the letter with you.
In my opinion the department has always been very co-operative. They have considered this matter and some changes have been made that are advantageous. There was a time when, because of circumstances, mail from Ottawa went through the Besserer street post office and was delayed there. In particular, mail in brown envelopes was not given very much consideration and was often delayed. Mail that was sent to the station and put on a train providing drop-off mail service was there in a matter of 12 hours, at the start of the next business day.
I hope the minister has looked into this matter. I know that the former minister was
[Mr. Peters.l
quite concerned about it, not only in terms of the service in relation to the operations of the Post Office Department itself, but with regard to the whole matter of railway mail service to small communities.

Item agreed to.
10. Transportation-movement of mail by land, air and water, including administration, $64,650,400.

On this item I also have another problem to raise with regard to the communities that do not have a large enough population to warrant the type of name and street directory published by private enterprise in the case of larger centres. In my area there has been a reluctance on the part of one postmaster in Kirkland Lake to give much consideration to mail. I would not say this was on a political basis, but he seems to think that anything coming from Ottawa is propaganda and therefore really does not deserve much consideration.
In this municipality we have a very large turnover of population because of the type of people who lives there. Mining communities have always had a large turnover, and although directories may be issued only two or three months before we are sending out a large quantity of mail, we have found that in some cases returned mail has amounted to as much as 18 per cent. We had discussions previously with the director of the department. At the time he was interested in establishing on a trial basis an I.B.M.6 system which would require the postmasters in the town to make out a form when mail was undelivered and return that form so the directories could be brought up to date.
Before the last election the situation in my riding was probably worse than in any other, and because of the fact that we tried to give such broad coverage we ascertained that there was no way of establishing where people had moved to. The director was kind enough to put out a temporary list at that time in mimeographed form and we used this. We found that after only a month had gone by there was a 4 or 5 per cent change in addresses.
I think the suggestion of the director is one that merits some consideration at least on a trial basis. An I.B.M. form would be used and every urban or rural carrier who could not deliver a letter would note the change of address. This form would be returned to the district post office and referred to the directory section at Ottawa so the change could be made there. This was contemplated, but I have not heard anything more about it. I presume the matter has been neglected. I suggest this is a field where the rural directory has been serving a purpose and has been used by businesses and others interested

in securing mail coverage in their area. I believe it should be maintained, and if it is going to be maintained it is not much more expensive to keep it up to date. It is unfortunate that some of the postmasters pay very little attention to this matter. I have checked in Ottawa and I find that the rural carriers outside the city have cards. When mail is being delivered they try to ascertain to where the person to whom it is addressed has moved. The changes are made so that the change of address finally gets back to the distribution point where sorting takes place, and something can be done there to remedy the situation. In the case of Kirkland Lake, all it amounted to was that we took off the list the people we knew did not live at the address to where their letters were being sent. As far as the directory is concerned Kirkland Lake is short two or three thousand people who live in that municipality. In this connection I think a punch card system could be tried on a rental basis in an effort to bring the matter up to date.
This problem may not be too important to members of parliament, because it is interesting to note that if a member of parliament sends out literature and it comes back he readdresses it to somebody else and sends it out again. But from the point of view of the businessman, if he is using the directory for the purpose of furthering his enterprise, I think this would be very disconcerting. Therefore I hope the minister will let us know whether he can give some consideration to the rural directories, because a large number of ridings in Canada are affected in the way I have described. I believe it is a worth-while service which, with a little more effort, could be brought more up to date than it has in the past. The director which the minister has in his department is doing as much as possible with the limited number of people he has; but this is a big department and should get more consideration than has been possible in the past.

I am rising to ask the minister to give careful consideration to a policy review in the department with respect to the present definitions or arrangements which would restrict the carrying of mails to scheduled carriers. I make this request with particular reference to the carriage of mails by air because of the very anomalous situations which may exist, and which certainly do exist on the west coast of Canada; reference was made earlier to this problem by the hon. member for Skeena.
By way of illustration I should point out that in actual fact much of the mail at the present time is carried on the coast by non-scheduled carriers. I happened to notice the
28902-5-388J
supply-Post Office
other day that a complete polling station in the last federal election, where the address of all the ^ electors in my constituency was provided, is listed as having an address in care of a certain air line, or one or two air lines. This is their postal address. Yet I know that neither of the particular air lines mentioned are officially carrying any mails. I do not know whether the Postmaster General remembers a discussion which took place in this house a number of years ago, when the esteemed late Mr. Cote was postmaster general, on the subject of what one member described as bootlegged mail. I very well recall how horrified was the then postmaster general at the suggestion that any of Her Majesty's mail was being bootlegged. I also recall that it was quite easy to tell where in the house those members who represented the more sparsely settled constituencies came from, because of the chortles of laughter which came from those particular spots in the house at the postmaster general declaring up and down that no such thing could possibly exist as the bootlegging of Her Majesty's mail.
I do^ know that, because of the present regulations, those in charge of trying to work out the best arrangement for the transportation of mails are often hamstrung, because of the existence of the regulations, in deciding what constitutes a scheduled carrier. I remember hearing recently the Minister of Transport say that he had discovered, while attending an international air conference that in many respects Canada has a system of air transportation which is quite unique in the world. Many of our communities since the advent of transportation by air have become dependant upon a form of transportation which really has no parallel anywhere else in the world. I feel that the present rules and regulations concerning the transportation of mails have not, as far as I can see, been altered very much since the time when all mails had to be transported either by rail, or by water in areas where steamer transportation existed.
Apart from having developed certain arrangements regarding the rapid transit of mails on the cross-Canada runs we really have not looked into the problem of how the mail services could be improved by making use of the smaller air lines which, in many cases, are operating under a class three or even under a charter form of licence. I feel the time has come when there should be a much more careful look at this question from the policy level in Ottawa in order that the officers of the department who are concerned with trying to provide the best transit of mails can do a better job.

Supply-Post Office
One of the considerations which the department tends to lose sight of is the community of interest in certain areas. There are areas in my constituency where it is a matter of a ten minute flight by air from one community to another, with planes running to and from these points quite frequently, but it takes at least a week for the transportation of mails. These are communities which are united in a geographic area of interest in such things as hospital districts, in such things as school districts, in such things as the administrative functioning of an Indian agency, where it is most difficult for ordinary business to be transacted within a reasonable period of time.
I have also had people complaining that they have practically been taken to court by the authorities in the provincial administration because they were not able to comply with certain provincial regulations regarding the filling out and return of certain forms and reports within a prescribed period of time. This is a problem which some of the smaller municipalities face in dealing with the department of municipal affairs in Victoria. I have discussed this matter from time to time with some of the officers of the department. I realize it is a very complex matter, one for which there is no easy or clearcut solution; but I feel that there should be a top policy review by the minister's department m Ottawa to see whether some better arrangements can be worked out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Before it carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like a reply from the minister as to what his functions are and what the department is going to do about the anticipated curtailment of trains 49 and 50, on the Toronto to Timmins service. The latest word I have is that it is the intention to drop this service entirely by April.

Mr. Chairman, in order to answer the question of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), I must say that I do not know how we will manage, if certain lines are abandoned. "We will then decide to organize the transportation of mail by land. I must emphasize here that we have done our best to obtain railway service, in order that a certain amount of mail could be carried by railway if the matter is not settled by trucking.

May I ask one question of the Postmaster General. I have given him warning of this question on previous occasions. I know there have been some unkind things said, but I want to wish the hon. gentleman a very merry Christmas. And I want to ask

him this: Would he mind explaining to the Canadian people and to the House of Commons why there have been no robberies since he took over his job of Postmaster General.

There have been some robberies since we took over, unfortunately, we have not had enough time to convince the thieves or robbers that they should change the bad habits they had formed under the previous regime.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That concludes the estimates of the Postmaster General's department.

Mr. Chairman, allow me to thank all hon. members and all those who contributed to the passage of my estimates. I thank them for the flowers, but somewhat less for the thorns. Fortunately, they were not too prickly and I think I can stand it.
However, with regard to my possible appointment to the Senate, it would be difficult for me to satisfy everybody. Some people want to send me to the other place, and others want to keep me here. I cannot cut myself in two and I suggest that the decision should be left to those responsible. Then we will know if the house loses or the Senate gains.

The Speaker of the Senate-*
2. Allowance in lieu of residence, $3,000.

This is a very important subject in my opinion and it is one which has not been looked at carefully for a long time. Many people do not realize the extent of the field which is covered by these estimates. The housekeeping of parliament has grown very greatly since the days when the Speaker and the Sergeant-at-Arms knew everyone by name. The time is ripe, in my opinion, when we should provide the house with a more efficient method of operation than we have been able to obtain under the present system. Most of the items under this heading, legislation, are handled, as hon. members are aware, by the officers of internal economy who include the Speaker and several members of the cabinet. We are all aware that most of the members of the eternal economy committee-
The eternal economy committee?
What is the matter with "eternal"?
You were right first time.

It may have developed to that point, and that is what I would like to change.
The operation of the House of Commons involves the equivalent of a town of fairly large size. There are, working here, more than 1,000 employees, and if 1,000 employees were working in a municipality, the operation of a municipality containing between 5,000 and 10,000 people would be provided for. It is true we do not have the responsibility for providing recreation for the children. We do not have many streets. We do not face a number of the problems with which a municipality has to contend. On the other hand, there are many which a municipality could avoid. The majority of the staff of the House of Commons do not come under direct control of the civil service. The staff employed in these buildings includes stenographers, messengers, protective officers, cleaners, employees of the Department of Public Works and, of course, members of parliament; but I suppose we would not include them, Mr. Chairman, in the working force. I suppose they amount to an additional 350 including the Senate.

You were talking about
workers.

Thus, we have a large number of people and it is doubtful whether an organization like this can best be handled under the system which was originally set up. I suggest the time has come when we should make changes. I should like to discuss some of the problems which face us and go into details about some of those problems in order that members may be aware of the situation which the Speaker has to face from day to day. I should like to spend some time commenting on the long range considerations which he has to bear in mind, and on the relationship which exists between the rules of this house and the actual operation. I should like to go into this question and make some suggestions for the consideration of the committee. I should like to call it seven o'clock and do all this at a later date when the estimates come before us again.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is not seven o'clock, and I hope the hon. member does not intend to deny me the right to say a word in the committee, too. The government, particularly to oblige the group to which the hon. member belongs, brought these particular estimates on at this time rather than at the usual time, at the very end of the estimates. This was done particularly to oblige the hon. gentleman. I may say that the other members of the committee enjoy listening to the hon. member and we would be willing to listen
Supply-Legislation
to him as long as he wants to talk about this matter. I suggest, therefore, that he accommodate the rest of us by getting right on with his speech.

I do not know what the Secretary of State is trying to do, but there has been no accommodation. These estimates were brought down at five minutes to seven. My hon. friend has a perfect right to call it seven o'clock and continue his speech whenever the estimates are before us again. We did ask that they be brought on sufficiently early to allow of discussion.
Why not get ahead now?

There is no reason why we should continue. We agreed to sit this morning at twelve o'clock. We agreed to sit until seven. I see no reason why we should extend this sitting beyond seven o'clock merely because the Secretary of State wants to rush these estimates through in a few minutes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think, on reflection, the hon. gentleman will consider that statement of his as being a most unfair one. I am not suggesting these estimates should be rushed through at all. What I said-and he can examine the words I used-was that I thought it was the sense of the whole committee that we were willing to sit here and listen to the hon. gentleman for as long as he wished to speak. That, surely, is not rushing anything. But there are 265 members in this house and some of us would like to get the business done in the present week. The hon. member has something he wants to say. We want to hear it. I do not know whether I am speaking for the committee generally, but I think I am, and I say to him: we are all ready to hear him for as long as he wants to go on, but we do ask him to make his speech now.

I think the Secretary of State is making some inaccurate assumptions. We have, as a group, agreed that there should be an extension of time as suggested. It was certainly not the responsibility of my hon. friend from Timiskaming that these particular estimates did not come before us until five minutes to seven. The Secretary of State is right when he says there are 265 members of this house all of whom have the right to bring up matters which are of interest to them. I do not mind confessing, Mr. Chairman, quite freely that much of the discussion that occupied a good deal of the time this afternoon I considered to be quite inconsequential to the functioning of parliament, and much less important than the subject matter the hon. member for Timiskaming was discussing. This is only my opinion, however, and I do not expect it to be shared by

Business of the House other members. I feel that I have been here and available during the hours that were set and that the hon. member for Timiska-ming is quite right in his contention.

It is seven o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext: May I now ask the house leader how much business he expects to get through the house tomorrow?

Do not accommodate me tomorrow.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Timiskaming for his courteous interruption. For reasons which I do not think I should bore the committee by going into, we would like to start tomorrow with the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture; then, take the estimates of the Minister of Fisheries; then, the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue, and then the estimates of His Honour the Speaker. We would then take the estimates of the Department of Labour. After that, it seems to me that I could perhaps ascertain from hon. members which departments it would be most suitable to bring on from that time forward.
I should like to say that I seem to have been misunderstood a few minutes ago. I do not wish in any way to reflect on any hon. member in anything I have said. I have been trying, sometimes with rather a lot of difficulty, to accommodate hon. members in all corners of the house about sittings and everything else. There has only been one occasion during this session when the government has had to make a motion and divide the house on the sitting hours. I should like to be able to do that for the rest of the week to the end of the session. I should like also to have the session end at the end of this week, as perhaps could be accomplished

because there have been very few sessions in the history of parliament when more time has been devoted to the consideration of the estimates than in the present session, if the hours are looked at. There have been a few, but not many. No one can say we have neglected consideration of these expenditures.
Now, of course, the Minister of National Defence will be back tomorrow as will the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The one department has only been discussed, but no items have been passed and the other is not completed. There are a number of other departments that have not been completed as yet. We cannot hope to conclude the proceedings this week without a certain degree of self-discipline. I do not believe, either, that because each of us thinks his speech is important, though some of us perhaps are occasionally resentful of those of others, we can accomplish our objective unless we are willing to make a serious extension of the hours. I am not going to ask now, but I hope tomorrow at the opening of the house there may be unanimous consent to sitting, from the opening of the sitting, without a break until some time late in the evening when there is a motion to adjourn.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: May I ask the Secretary of State whether there is any other legislation to come before this session? As a subheading, I mention the world's fair bill and the two or three Senate bills to which he referred earlier. Are those items still on the agenda or have they been dropped?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
So far as the three bills from the Senate are concerned, which I believe are non-contentious, I hope the house would be able to find time after the estimates have been concluded to consider them. I have said two or three times, that we are not going to hold up prorogation if they are not considered. However, they would have to be started all over again and they would take up a certain amount of the time of both houses at the next session if we do not consider them now. Hon. members have had these bills on their files for some time, and I believe they realize they would not need prolonged discussion.
In so far as the world's fair bill is concerned, the reason we did not proceed earlier is that there were discussions going on earlier this week which might have necessitated some slight amendment to the bill. I did not want to waste the time of the house by bringing it up until we were sure. I am not able to say for certain, but it may be we will have to take time to consider it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
May I ask one other question? Has the Secretary of State in mind suggesting any additional extension of hours,

bearing in mind that he has done fairly well at this session by consultation and by getting co-operation? He has done rather well, has he not? It may be a good idea to continue with this, rather than just bringing it to the house cold.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As a matter of fact, I thought I made it very clear in what I said earlier-perhaps I did not-that I was not asking the consent of the house now to the hours for tomorrow. I do not want to take hon. members by surprise. If I could get consent now, I cannot tell you how happy I would be. I am not asking for it. I am hoping hon. members will reflect upon it between now and the time of meeting at eleven o'clock tomorrow. Then at eleven o'clock tomorrow I could propose that an order be made that the house remain in session continuously throughout the day until a motion is made for adjournment, which would certainly be made before the end of that day.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I just ask the house leader if he will reconsider the proposed legislation that is still to come before us? So far as we are concerned we do not want to be put in the position of having to consider legislation at the conclusion of the estimates. We would rather deal with it before the estimates are concluded.
The reason I say that, is that the official opposition has shown as much desire as the government side to get the business of the house completed, but it is not in our mind at the moment that we would like to sit late, say, on Saturday or Sunday morning to consider some piece of legislation which we ourselves might not wish to debate at any great length. Much as we would like to accommodate other parties in the house, there is obviously a limit.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
With respect to the
measure regarding the world fair, just as soon as the government is in a position to bring it forward, and that will not be tomorrow-but it might conceivably be the first item on Friday-just as soon as we are in a position to say definitely what we will do about it, I will indicate it through the usual channels to hon. gentlemen, and it would be our view it should be brought forward early, because it is legislation that has to pass both houses. These other small measures respecting the Department of Transport have already been through the other place. After we send the appropriations bill to the other place there is always a certain interval, and if they do not pass it in that interval we would not hold up prorogation if they had not passed it; but if it could be-
National Harbours Board Act

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: We could have done all this in the time we are talking about it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then I am prepared to propose them right now and get them disposed of. Do we have unanimous consent to do that, sir?
Agreed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The three are the Ontario harbours bill, the national harbours bill, and the carriage by air act.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right. If you would call item No. 4 on today's order paper we could proceed.

speechtext: I would like to ask the house leader if he wants me to check the French version of this bill, or will he leave it to the hon. member for Lapointe?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I am sure the Secretary of State would like to be able to answer another question so that he can show what a good mood he is now in. Is it clear that the only other piece of legislation for this session, apart from the appropriations bill, would be the one regarding the world fair?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is a very embarrassing question. I do not know whether the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knows quite how embarrassing it is, but I believe in certain quarters of the house there have been some discussions about a number of private bills that are on the order paper and a method of disposing of them, about which an understanding has not yet been reached. It may be that as the result of certain consultations that are going on if all hon. members of the house were agreeable there might be some method found of dealing with that problem.
Mr. Speaker, we are only asking the minister about government legislation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am referring also to government legislation.
May I ask the minister, what additional government legislation?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It would be a measure providing for another method of dealing with those private bills that are now on the order paper. But really I would prefer not to go into any more explanations at this time, because these discussions have not advanced very far and they may come to nothing.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Just tell us you are in a good mood.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know how many hon. members heard the program this morning that comes on right after the news at eight o'clock-it is one of my favourite programs-in which a speech from the throne was delivered by one of our friends who sit above us and observe us from a lofty eminence. It was said in that broadcast that I had expressed appreciation-perhaps the extent of it was exaggerated a little bit-for the cooperation of the opposition. I must say that I do think that in so far as the management of the house is concerned, the co-operation of the opposition ever since September 30-I say nothing about the early part of the session-in the difficult circumstances of this particular parliament has been very good indeed, and I continue to say so.
Hear, hear.
